choices: Run makemigrations before startapp — the app tables must exist before the app code
Add the new app's config class to INSTALLED_APPS in settings.py, then run makemigrations and migrate
Copy the app directory into the project root — Django auto-discovers apps on the filesystem
Run collectstatic so the app's models are registered with the ORM
evidence:
$ python manage.py startapp inventory
$ python manage.py makemigrations inventory
No changes detected in app 'inventory'
scenarios.hint: startapp created the code. What tells Django's app registry that this app exists?
scenarios.prompt: Why does Django not see the app, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: After running startapp and writing models, makemigrations reports 'No changes detected' for the new app.
scenarios.title: The invisible app
scenarios.why: startapp only scaffolds files; Django's app registry learns about the app through INSTALLED_APPS in settings.py (add 'inventory' or 'inventory.apps.InventoryConfig'). Until then, the ORM, migrations, and admin all ignore it. This ordering — startapp, register, then makemigrations — is the standard new-app checklist.

choices: Set FLASK_APP=shop:create_app and run flask run — the CLI can call a factory when given app:factory
Flask 3 removed the app factory pattern; define the app at module level instead
Factories only work with flask shell, not flask run
Rename create_app to make_app — flask run looks for that exact name
evidence:
def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.register_blueprint(bp)
    return app

# no module-level `app` object

$ flask run
Error: Could not import 'shop'.
scenarios.hint: The CLI needs to know which callable builds the app. What syntax lets you name a module and a factory function?
scenarios.prompt: How do you run this app with the Flask CLI?
scenarios.situation: A Flask project uses the application factory pattern (create_app) with no module-level app object, and flask run can't find the app.
scenarios.title: The CLI can't find the app
scenarios.why: The Flask CLI imports the value of FLASK_APP. With a factory, you point it at the callable using the module:factory syntax — FLASK_APP=shop:create_app (optionally with arguments, e.g. shop:create_app('development')). The factory pattern stays valuable for testing and multiple instances; you just have to tell the CLI where the factory lives.

choices: requirements.txt is only read by pip install -r on Windows; on Linux use setup.py
The venv wasn't activated when pip install ran, so packages went to the system Python — activate the venv first, then reinstall
Flask must be installed with apt, not pip, on Debian-based systems
The project needs a Pipfile — requirements.txt is deprecated and ignored
evidence:
$ python -m venv .venv
$ pip install -r requirements.txt
$ .venv/bin/python -c "import flask"
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'flask'
scenarios.hint: `pip` and `.venv/bin/python` — are they necessarily the same Python? What determines which one `pip` points to?
scenarios.situation: A developer creates a venv and installs requirements, but the venv's Python can't import the packages.
scenarios.title: Installed nowhere
scenarios.why: pip resolved to a different Python than the venv's — the venv was created but never activated, so pip installed into the system (or another) environment. The robust fixes: activate the venv first, or bypass the ambiguity entirely with .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt, which guarantees the packages land in that interpreter.

choices: Set DEBUG=False — the debug toolbar blocks model imports
The models.py file must be named model.py (singular) for autodiscovery
The app is missing from INSTALLED_APPS or the import path is wrong — fix INSTALLED_APPS and check for circular imports
Run migrate with --fake-initial to register the models
evidence:
$ python manage.py shell
>>> from inventory.models import Product
ImportError: cannot import name 'Product' from 'inventory.models'
scenarios.hint: Django found the module but not the name. Is this a Django problem — or does the class simply not exist where you think it does?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
scenarios.situation: Importing a model in the Django shell fails even though inventory/models.py exists.
scenarios.title: The model that isn't there
scenarios.why: This is usually a plain Python import problem, not a Django one: the class name is misspelled, the model was defined in a different file, or there's a circular import (models importing from views that import models). Check the class actually exists in that module, then look at INSTALLED_APPS and import cycles. --fake-initial is for migration state, not missing classes.

choices: Each developer runs pip install on their own machine whenever something breaks — fastest
Commit requirements.txt (pinned versions) and document venv setup; consider pip-tools or a lock file so installs are reproducible
Email the site-packages directory to new team members
Install everything with --user so all projects share one environment
evidence:
$ pip freeze | head -5
Django==5.0.4
Django==5.1.2
# two developers, two different Django versions, one broken deploy
scenarios.hint: What artifact makes 'works on my machine' reproducible on every machine — and what makes it trustworthy?
scenarios.prompt: What practice prevents this class of problem?
scenarios.situation: Two developers have different Django versions installed; staging breaks with an error nobody sees locally.
scenarios.title: Works on my machine
scenarios.why: Unpinned, unshared dependencies make every environment a snowflake. A committed requirements file with pinned versions (pip freeze or, better, pip-tools compile producing a lock file) plus a documented venv setup makes installs deterministic. Shared --user installs and emailed site-packages are the opposite of reproducible.

choices: Delete the migrations directory and re-run makemigrations — a clean slate is safest
Edit the old migration file by hand to add the field
Create a new migration with makemigrations, review the generated operations, then migrate — never edit applied migrations
Run migrate --fake so Django believes the field exists without touching the database
evidence:
$ python manage.py makemigrations
Migrations for 'shop':
  shop/migrations/0003_order_status.py
    + Add field status to order
scenarios.hint: The migration was generated but the database doesn't have the column yet. Which command pair completes the job — and why shouldn't you hand-edit history?
scenarios.prompt: What are the correct next steps?
scenarios.situation: A developer adds a field to a model and generates a migration, but the column still doesn't exist in the database.
scenarios.title: The migration that didn't migrate
scenarios.why: makemigrations only writes the migration file; migrate applies it to the database. Both steps are required. And applied migrations are shared history — editing them breaks every other environment; new changes get new migrations. --fake is for reconciling state Django already believes, not for skipping real schema changes.

choices: Add the converter to INSTALLED_APPS so Django loads the int type
Use <int:year> in the path — path converters validate and convert the segment, returning 404 for non-integers
Wrap the view in try/except ValueError — converters can't validate URL segments
Use re_path with a regex — path() doesn't support typed segments
evidence:
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('archive/<year>/', views.year_archive),
]

def year_archive(request, year):
    # year arrives as a string; /archive/abcd/ should 404 but doesn't
scenarios.hint: `path()` supports typed placeholders like `<int:year>`. What do they do to a non-matching segment?
scenarios.prompt: How should the URL pattern enforce the type?
scenarios.situation: An archive URL should only match numeric years, but /archive/abcd/ currently reaches the view instead of 404ing.
scenarios.title: The year that wasn't a number
scenarios.why: path() converters (<int:year>, <slug:slug>, <uuid:pk>, <str:name>, <path:rest>) both validate the segment and convert it to the Python type before the view runs; non-matching URLs fall through to a 404. Without a converter, every segment is a string and validation becomes manual view code.

choices: Use url_for('admin.dashboard') — url_for takes the endpoint name, which for blueprints is blueprint_name.view_function
Use url_for('dashboard') — blueprint names are stripped from endpoints
Hardcode '/admin/' — url_for can't reverse blueprint routes
Use url_for('bp.dashboard') — the endpoint uses the blueprint's variable name
evidence: werkzeug.routing.BuildError: Could not build url for endpoint 'dashboard'
scenarios.hint: The error names the endpoint it looked for. What does Flask actually register the endpoint as when the view lives on a blueprint?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct url_for call?
scenarios.situation: url_for('dashboard') raises BuildError even though the dashboard view exists on the admin blueprint.
scenarios.title: The endpoint that moved
scenarios.why: When a view is registered on a blueprint named 'admin', its endpoint becomes 'admin.dashboard' — the blueprint name prefixes the function name. url_for must use the full endpoint. (The url_prefix affects the URL path, not the endpoint name — a common confusion.)

choices: request.data — form posts arrive as raw bytes
request.form.get('email') — POSTed form fields live in request.form; request.args is only for query strings
request.args.get('email') — Flask merges form data into args automatically
request.json['email'] — browsers send forms as JSON by default
scenarios.hint: The HTML form posts with method=POST. Where does the parsed body go — args, form, or json?
scenarios.situation: A newsletter form POSTs an email field, but the view reads None.
scenarios.title: Looking in the wrong bag
scenarios.why: request.args holds the query string (?a=b in the URL); request.form holds parsed POST form bodies; request.get_json() handles JSON payloads. Reading request.args for a form POST always yields None. Matching the accessor to the content type is the entire fix.

choices: Return the dict directly — Django serializes any return value to JSON
Return JsonResponse({'items': items}) — and ensure datetimes/Decimals are serialized to JSON-safe types first
Use HttpResponse with content_type='application/json' and pass the dict as the body
JsonResponse only accepts lists; wrap the dict in a list
scenarios.hint: The error names the type that broke serialization. Where is the right place to convert it — the query, the view, or the response class?
scenarios.situation: A JSON API view crashes serializing Decimal prices from the database.
scenarios.title: The price that wouldn't serialize
scenarios.why: Python's json module can't serialize Decimal (or datetime) — JsonResponse uses DjangoJSONEncoder, which handles datetimes but not Decimals. Convert at the boundary: str(price) or float(price) in the view/serializer, or use values() with an annotated string cast. The principle: serialize to JSON-safe types before handing data to the response.

choices: Redirects must be returned from middleware; views can only return 200 responses
Return redirect('cart') (or HttpResponseRedirect) — the POST/Redirect/GET pattern prevents duplicate submissions on refresh
Render the cart template directly with a 200 — the URL doesn't matter
Use redirect() but with status_code=200 so the browser stays on the same page
scenarios.hint: What does the browser do when the user refreshes a page that was the direct response to a POST?
scenarios.prompt: What pattern prevents the double order?
scenarios.situation: After checkout, refreshing the confirmation page re-submits the order and charges the customer twice.
scenarios.title: The double-charged refresh
scenarios.why: Rendering a 200 response directly to a POST leaves the POST as the current page — refresh replays it. POST/Redirect/GET returns a 302 redirect after the POST, so the browser GETs the confirmation page; refreshing then repeats only the harmless GET. Django's redirect() shortcut implements this in one line.

choices: Register the 404 handler with @app.errorhandler(404) returning the template and a 404 status — error handlers are per-status-code functions
Raise a custom exception in every view — Flask has no central 404 handling
Return the template with status 200 from a catch-all route — the status code doesn't matter for error pages
404 handling requires the Flask-Debug extension
scenarios.hint: Flask lets you register a function for an HTTP status code. What decorator maps 404 to your template?
scenarios.prompt: How do you serve a branded 404 page?
scenarios.situation: abort(404) shows Flask's default plain error page; the site needs a branded template.
scenarios.title: The default-looking 404
scenarios.why: @app.errorhandler(404) registers a function that Flask calls for that status code; returning (render_template('404.html'), 404) serves the branded page with the correct status. The status matters — returning 200 would tell search engines and clients the missing page exists.

choices: Use on_delete=models.DO_NOTHING — the database enforces referential integrity automatically
Use on_delete=models.CASCADE so deleting an author deletes their books; Django requires an explicit on_delete on every ForeignKey
ForeignKeys don't need on_delete in Django 5 — it defaults to CASCADE
Use on_delete=models.SET_NULL without null=True — Django fills in NULL automatically
scenarios.hint: Django forces you to state the deletion rule explicitly. Which rule matches 'an author deletion removes their books'?
scenarios.prompt: Which on_delete behavior fits, and why is the argument required?
scenarios.situation: A Book belongs to an Author. Deleting an author should remove their books, and the ForeignKey definition is incomplete.
scenarios.title: The orphaned books
scenarios.why: Django requires on_delete on every ForeignKey so deletion semantics are always a conscious choice: CASCADE deletes dependents, PROTECT blocks the deletion, SET_NULL keeps the row with a null FK (needs null=True), SET_DEFAULT, or DO_NOTHING. Leaving it out is a hard error, not a default — the framework refuses to guess about data loss.

choices: QuerySets hit the database when defined, so the loop is fine — the problem is the template
Each iteration issues a query (N+1) — use select_related('author') on the queryset to fetch books with their authors in one JOIN
Add db_index=True to the title field — indexes eliminate N+1 queries
Convert the queryset to a list() before the loop — materializing it batches the queries
scenarios.hint: 501 queries for 500 books: one for the list, then one per book. What does accessing `book.author` trigger — and how do you fetch it up front?
scenarios.prompt: What causes the 501 queries, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: A book list page issues 501 database queries for 500 books.
scenarios.title: Five hundred books, five hundred queries
scenarios.why: Accessing book.author on each iteration lazily fires one query per book — the N+1 problem. select_related('author') follows the ForeignKey with a SQL JOIN, loading authors in the initial query. (prefetch_related is the counterpart for reverse FK and many-to-many relations, which need separate queries.) The debug toolbar's query count is the standard way to spot this.

choices: Book.objects.filter(title__contains='django') — contains is case-insensitive by default
Book.objects.filter(title__icontains='django') — icontains is the case-insensitive containment lookup
Book.objects.search(title='django') — the ORM has a dedicated search method
Book.objects.filter(title='django') — exact match handles substrings automatically
evidence:
>>> Book.objects.filter(title__contains='django').count()
3
>>> # but 'Django Unleashed' (capital D) is missing from results
scenarios.hint: The lookup is `contains` and the missing row differs only by case. Which lookup variant ignores case?
scenarios.prompt: Which lookup finds the title regardless of case?
scenarios.situation: A search for 'django' misses 'Django Unleashed' because the lookup is case-sensitive.
scenarios.title: The case of the missing book
scenarios.why: Django field lookups come in case-sensitive/case-insensitive pairs: contains/icontains, exact/iexact, startswith/istartswith. contains maps to LIKE (case behavior depends on the database collation — Postgres LIKE is case-sensitive), while icontains forces case-insensitive matching. Picking the right variant is part of writing correct queries, not just fast ones.

choices: Wrap the loop in a transaction with db.session.begin() — actually Flask-SQLAlchemy already wraps each request in a transaction; the bug is the missing db.session.commit() after the loop
Call db.session.flush() after each add — flush writes to the database permanently
Create a new db.session per iteration — sessions can't track multiple new objects
Replace add() with merge() — add() only works for existing rows
scenarios.hint: The objects were staged but never finalized. What call turns staged changes into a durable transaction?
scenarios.prompt: Why is the table empty after the import?
scenarios.situation: A bulk import adds hundreds of objects to the session, but nothing persists.
scenarios.title: The import that vanished
scenarios.why: db.session.add() only stages objects in the unit of work; nothing reaches the database until db.session.commit(). Without commit, the transaction is rolled back when the session closes. (flush() sends SQL but doesn't commit — useful for getting IDs mid-transaction, not for durability.)

choices: Add unique=True to the email field — the ORM validates uniqueness before saving
Catch the IntegrityError from the database — uniqueness is enforced at the database level; validate in the form AND handle the race at the DB
Check User.objects.filter(email=email).exists() first — that fully prevents duplicates
Uniqueness can't be enforced on emails; use usernames instead
scenarios.hint: Two requests can both pass the exists() check at the same instant. What is the final arbiter — and what exception does it raise?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct duplicate-handling strategy?
scenarios.situation: Email must be unique. A pre-save exists() check still lets occasional duplicates through under load.
scenarios.title: The duplicate that slipped through
scenarios.why: An exists() check followed by an insert is a check-then-act race: two concurrent requests can both see 'no such email' and both insert. The database unique constraint is the real enforcement — it raises IntegrityError on the loser. The correct pattern: validate early in the form for a friendly message, and catch IntegrityError at save time for the race. unique=True creates the constraint; it doesn't replace handling the exception.

choices: Order.objects.all().delete() then re-create — simplest and safe
Use update() on the queryset: Order.objects.filter(status='pending').update(status='shipped') — one SQL UPDATE, no per-object save
Loop over orders and call order.save() — the ORM batches saves automatically
Use bulk_create with the new status — bulk operations handle updates too
evidence:
# 20,000 pending orders need status='shipped'
orders = Order.objects.filter(status='pending')
for o in orders:
    o.status = 'shipped'
    o.save()  # 20k UPDATEs, signals fire, slow
scenarios.hint: You don't need Python objects at all — just 'set this column where that condition holds'. Which queryset method maps to a single UPDATE?
scenarios.situation: Marking 20,000 orders as shipped with a save() loop takes minutes.
scenarios.title: Twenty thousand UPDATEs
scenarios.why: QuerySet.update() issues a single SQL UPDATE for the whole filtered set — no object instantiation, no per-row save. The loop materializes 20k objects and fires 20k UPDATEs (plus save signals). Trade-off to know: update() skips model save() methods and signals, so it's for pure data changes, not logic that lives in save(). (bulk_create is the insert counterpart.)

choices: Add {% csrf_token %} inside the <form> — Django's CsrfViewMiddleware rejects POSTs without the token (403)
Add @csrf_exempt to the view — CSRF protection is opt-in per view
CSRF only applies to AJAX requests; plain form POSTs are exempt
Set CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE=False — the token is blocked by the secure flag
scenarios.hint: The 403 names the failure: CSRF verification. What must the template include so the POST carries proof it came from your site?
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, and why does Django reject the POST?
scenarios.situation: A plain HTML form POST returns 403 'CSRF verification failed.'
scenarios.title: The form Django wouldn't trust
scenarios.why: Django's CsrfViewMiddleware requires POSTs to carry a token proving the request originated from your own pages (defense against cross-site request forgery). {% csrf_token %} renders the hidden input; without it, the middleware 403s. @csrf_exempt disables the protection — the fix for a broken form is the token, not the exemption.

choices: {{ review.text }} is already safe — Django escapes everything including the script tags, so no change needed
Django autoescapes {{ }} output by default, neutralizing the script — only the |safe filter or mark_safe would make it dangerous; verify no |safe is applied
Switch to {% autoescape off %} for performance — escaping is redundant with the ORM
Store the review as JSON instead of text — JSON can't contain scripts
scenarios.hint: What does Django's template engine do to `<` and `>` inside `{{ }}` by default — and which filter would undo it?
scenarios.prompt: Is the page vulnerable, and what must be checked?
scenarios.situation: A user submits a review containing a script tag. The template renders {{ review.text }}.
scenarios.title: The review with a script tag
scenarios.why: Django autoescapes variable output by default: <script> becomes <script> and renders as inert text. The page is safe as written — the danger enters only if someone applies |safe or mark_safe to user content. The review checklist: user content must never pass through |safe; that's the single gate between data and code execution here.

choices: Read request.POST directly in the view — forms are just HTML
Define a forms.Form (or ModelForm), instantiate with request.POST, call is_valid(), then use cleaned_data — validation, type conversion, and errors come free
Validation belongs in JavaScript; the server should trust the POST body
Use a ModelForm but skip is_valid() — saving directly is faster
scenarios.hint: `request.POST` values are all strings, and 'abc' isn't a guest count. What Django object turns raw POST data into validated, converted Python values?
scenarios.situation: A view reads request.POST directly; invalid input crashes with ValueError and there's no error display.
scenarios.title: Parsing POST by hand
scenarios.why: Django forms encapsulate the whole input pipeline: field types convert strings to Python values (IntegerField rejects 'abc'), validators enforce rules, is_valid() gates processing, cleaned_data provides the converted values, and the form re-renders with per-field errors. Hand-parsing request.POST reimplements all of this badly. ModelForm goes further, binding directly to a model for create/update views.

choices: Jinja2 autoescapes nothing — every variable must be manually escaped with |e
Jinja2 autoescapes template variables by default in Flask; use |safe only for content you generated and trust, never for user input
Flask disables autoescaping when render_template is used; only render_template_string escapes
Autoescape applies only to variables, so {{ user.bio|safe }} is the recommended way to render bios
scenarios.hint: Flask's render_template uses Jinja2 with autoescape on. Which filter would a developer add to 'fix' HTML showing as text — and why is that the vulnerability?
scenarios.prompt: A teammate suggests adding |safe to render the bio 'properly'. What is the risk?
scenarios.situation: A user bio containing HTML renders as literal text. A teammate proposes |safe to 'fix' it.
scenarios.title: The 'fix' that opens the door
scenarios.why: Jinja2 autoescapes {{ }} output in Flask templates, so HTML in the bio shows as harmless text — that's the protection working. |safe marks content as trusted HTML, and applying it to user input re-enables stored XSS. The safe alternatives: keep escaping, or sanitize with a library like bleach allowing only specific tags. |safe is for markup your own code generated.

choices: Instantiate the form with the object (UserForm(obj=user)), validate, then form.populate_obj(user) and commit — WTForms maps fields back onto the model
Manually assign each field from request.form to the user — populate_obj is deprecated
Forms can't edit existing objects; delete and recreate the user
Use form.data dict directly as SQL SET values
scenarios.hint: WTForms forms accept an `obj` to read initial values from. What method writes validated data back onto that object?
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard edit pattern?
scenarios.situation: An edit page must pre-fill a form from an existing user and save changes on submit.
scenarios.title: The edit form, both directions
scenarios.why: The WTForms edit pattern is symmetric: pass obj=user on GET so fields pre-fill from the model; on a valid POST, form.populate_obj(user) writes each field back onto the same object, then db.session.commit(). This avoids hand-assigning dozens of fields and keeps validation in one place. (Flask-WTF adds CSRF protection to the form automatically.)

choices: Template inheritance is unavailable in Django — duplicate the markup per page
Create base.html with {% block content %}{% endblock %}, have each page {% extends 'base.html' %} and override the block — shared nav/footer live in one place
Use {% include %} for every page — includes support block overriding
Put the nav in a context processor — context processors render HTML blocks
evidence:
about.html, contact.html, pricing.html
# each file repeats the same 40-line <nav> and <footer>
scenarios.hint: You need a skeleton with named holes that child templates fill. Which two tags define the skeleton and the filling?
scenarios.prompt: How should the duplication be eliminated?
scenarios.situation: Every page template repeats the same nav and footer markup.
scenarios.title: Forty lines, three times
scenarios.why: {% extends %} / {% block %} is Django's layout mechanism: base.html defines the skeleton with named blocks, child templates override only what differs. {% include %} composes static partials but can't be overridden per page; context processors supply variables, not markup. Inheritance keeps one canonical nav/footer.

choices: Store the password in a CharField and compare strings directly — simplest and fastest
Hash with make_password() on registration and verify with check_password() on login — Django's default PBKDF2 hasher with per-password salts
Encrypt passwords with AES so support can decrypt them for users who forget
Hash with MD5 — it's fast and produces short hashes
evidence:
def register(request):
    # TODO: store the password securely
    user = User(username=username, password=???)
    user.save()
scenarios.hint: What property must the stored value have so that a database leak doesn't hand over every password — and who should never be able to reverse it, including you?
scenarios.prompt: How should the password be stored?
scenarios.situation: A custom registration view needs to store user passwords.
scenarios.title: Storing passwords
scenarios.why: Passwords must be stored as salted, deliberately-slow hashes — Django's make_password (PBKDF2 by default) handles salting, iteration count, and algorithm upgrades. check_password verifies without ever reversing the hash. Plaintext storage, reversible encryption, and fast hashes like MD5 all fail the moment the database leaks: fast hashes fall to brute force in hours.

choices: Query the User table manually and set request.user by hand
Call authenticate() to verify credentials, then login() to establish the session — and protect views with @login_required
Store the user id in a cookie directly — sessions are overkill
Authentication is automatic once the User model exists
evidence:
def sign_in(request):
    # TODO: verify username/password and start a session
scenarios.hint: Two steps: prove who they are, then remember it across requests. Which two Django functions do those jobs?
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard sign-in implementation?
scenarios.situation: A sign-in view must verify credentials and keep the user logged in across requests.
scenarios.title: Proving who they are
scenarios.why: authenticate(username=..., password=...) checks credentials against the configured backends and returns the user (or None); login(request, user) then persists the identity in the session. The pair is the standard flow — hand-rolled cookie user-ids skip session signing, rotation, and backend abstraction. @login_required on protected views completes the triangle.

choices: f"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = '{q}'" — f-strings are the modern way to build SQL
"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = %s", [q] — parameterized queries keep user input as data, never code
"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = '" + q.replace("'", "''") + "'" — manual escaping is sufficient
Raw SQL is banned in Django; rewrite everything with the ORM
evidence:
def search(request):
    q = request.GET.get('q', '')
    with connection.cursor() as c:
        c.execute(f"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{q}%'")
        rows = c.fetchall()
scenarios.hint: What happens when `q` contains `%' OR '1'='1` — and whose job is it to separate code from data?
scenarios.prompt: What is the vulnerability, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: A raw-SQL search view interpolates the query string directly into the SQL.
scenarios.title: The search box that reads the whole database
scenarios.why: String-interpolating user input into SQL is textbook SQL injection: crafted input escapes the string literal and rewrites the query. Parameterized queries (placeholders + params list) send the SQL and the values separately, so input can never become code. The ORM parameterizes automatically; raw SQL must do it by hand. Manual escaping is fragile and incomplete.

choices: Set SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=False so JavaScript can refresh the session
Ensure the session cookie uses HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Lax (Django defaults) and serve the site over HTTPS — stolen cookies are the target
Store the session id in localStorage for easier access from the frontend
Disable CSRF middleware — it interferes with session cookies
evidence:
SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE = 'Lax'
# TODO: is this the right hardening?
scenarios.hint: XSS steals cookies via JavaScript; network sniffing steals them in transit; cross-site forms ride them. Which flag counters each?
scenarios.prompt: Are these the right settings, and what does each defend against?
scenarios.situation: A security review asks about session cookie hardening for a Django site.
scenarios.title: Hardening the session cookie
scenarios.why: These are Django's secure defaults and each flag counters a real attack: HttpOnly blocks JavaScript access (blunts XSS cookie theft), Secure restricts the cookie to HTTPS (blocks network sniffing), SameSite=Lax stops the browser sending it on cross-site top-level navigations (blunts CSRF). Moving the session id to localStorage would expose it to any XSS; disabling CSRF middleware removes a layer for no gain.

choices: generate_password_hash() at registration and check_password_hash() at login — Werkzeug's default scrypt-based hashing with salts
hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() — SHA-256 is a standard
Store the password with Fernet encryption so it can be recovered
Compare plaintext — the database is behind a firewall
scenarios.hint: Same rule as Django: the stored value must survive a database leak. Which function produces a salted, slow hash?
scenarios.prompt: How should the password be stored and verified?
scenarios.situation: A Flask registration view needs secure password storage.
scenarios.title: Hashing in Flask
scenarios.why: Werkzeug's generate_password_hash produces a salted, adaptive hash (scrypt by default in Werkzeug 3); check_password_hash verifies against it. Fast hashes like SHA-256 are brute-forced with GPUs, encryption is reversible by design (wrong tool), and 'behind a firewall' is not a security boundary — breaches happen, and the hash is the last line of defense.

choices: Flask-Login is only for OAuth; use session['user_id'] manually for password logins
Use Flask-Login: LoginManager, a user_loader callback, login_user() on success, and @login_required on protected views
Store the whole user object in the session — sessions can hold any Python object
Authentication requires Flask-Security-Too; Flask-Login is deprecated
evidence:
from flask_login import LoginManager, login_user, login_required

login_manager = LoginManager(app)

# TODO: wire up user loading and protected routes
scenarios.hint: The login manager needs to turn a session-stored id back into a user object. Which callback provides that?
scenarios.prompt: What are the pieces of a working Flask-Login setup?
scenarios.situation: A Flask app needs login sessions and protected routes.
scenarios.title: Sessions in Flask
scenarios.why: Flask-Login's contract has four parts: a LoginManager bound to the app, a @login_manager.user_loader callback that maps the session's user id back to a User, login_user(user) after credential verification to establish the session, and @login_required guarding views. Hand-rolled session['user_id'] skips remember-me handling, session protection, and the unauthorized handler — the extension exists precisely to get these right.

choices: Run python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:80 — the dev server handles production traffic fine
Serve with gunicorn (WSGI server, multiple workers) behind nginx as a reverse proxy — runserver is single-threaded, insecure, and reloads code per request in debug
Run the app with flask run --host=0.0.0.0 — it's the same as gunicorn
Serve static files from Django and skip the reverse proxy to reduce moving parts
evidence:
$ python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000
# site is live; traffic is growing; responses are slow and static files 404 intermittently
scenarios.hint: What does runserver's own startup message warn about — and what two roles (app server vs. web server) does production need?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this production setup?
scenarios.situation: A Django site is served with runserver in production and struggles under load.
scenarios.title: The dev server in production
scenarios.why: runserver is a development convenience: single-threaded, no security hardening, inefficient static handling, and it literally warns against production use. Production Django is gunicorn (or uvicorn for ASGI) running the WSGI callable with multiple workers, behind nginx handling TLS termination, static files, and request buffering. Each layer does the job it's built for.

choices: Set DEBUG=False, set ALLOWED_HOSTS to the real domain(s), and load SECRET_KEY (and other secrets) from environment variables
Keep DEBUG=True so tracebacks help diagnose production errors faster
Set ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] for flexibility across domains
Commit the SECRET_KEY to the repo so all deploys share it
scenarios.hint: Three problems: verbose error pages leak internals, empty ALLOWED_HOSTS rejects every host once DEBUG is off, and a committed secret isn't secret. What's the production trio?
scenarios.prompt: What must change before this goes live?
scenarios.situation: Settings still carry development values as the first production deploy approaches.
scenarios.title: Dev settings go live
scenarios.why: Production Django needs the trio: DEBUG=False (tracebacks leak settings, paths, and queries), ALLOWED_HOSTS set to the real hostnames (Django 400s everything else once DEBUG is off — Host header attack defense), and SECRET_KEY plus DB credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager, never committed. ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] and committed secrets each quietly undo one of these protections.

choices: Static files are served from each app's static/ directory automatically in production
Run collectstatic to gather all static files into STATIC_ROOT, and have nginx (or WhiteNoise) serve that directory — Django doesn't serve static in production
Commit node_modules to STATIC_ROOT — collectstatic needs the sources
Set STATIC_URL to the database DSN so files stream from Postgres
evidence:
$ python manage.py collectstatic
132 files copied to '/var/www/static'.
scenarios.hint: Django's staticfiles app finds files across apps in development. What assembles them into one servable directory for production — and who should serve it?
scenarios.prompt: What does collectstatic do, and who serves the result?
scenarios.situation: Static assets work locally but 404 in production.
scenarios.title: The missing CSS
scenarios.why: In development Django serves static files per app; in production (DEBUG=False) it serves none. collectstatic copies every app's static files into the single STATIC_ROOT directory, which the web tier serves directly — nginx, a CDN, or WhiteNoise middleware. Pointing Django at the database or committing build artifacts are both category errors.

choices: Migrations run automatically when gunicorn starts — no step needed
Run migrations by hand on the production database whenever someone remembers
Run migrate as a distinct deploy step (release phase / CI job) before the new code serves traffic — code and schema must stay in sync
Delete and recreate the database on each deploy so the schema is always fresh
scenarios.hint: The new code expects the new column. If the code starts serving before the column exists, what happens — and what ordering prevents it?
scenarios.prompt: Where do migrations belong in the deploy?
scenarios.situation: A deploy script starts gunicorn but never runs migrations; new code crashes on missing columns.
scenarios.title: Code without its schema
scenarios.why: migrate must run as an explicit deploy step before the new code takes traffic — migrations are what keep the schema in lockstep with the models the code was written against. Gunicorn doesn't run them; manual 'whenever someone remembers' drifts; recreating the database destroys data. (For zero-downtime deploys, the advanced form is expand-then-contract migrations, but the baseline is: migrate before serving.)

choices: Use app.run(debug=True, host='0.0.0.0') in production — the reloader keeps workers fresh
Serve the Flask app with gunicorn (e.g. gunicorn 'myapp:create_app()') behind a reverse proxy; app.run is a development server
Flask apps can't use gunicorn — only Django can
Increase the thread count of app.run to match CPU cores
evidence:
from myapp import create_app
app = create_app()
scenarios.hint: `app.run` is documented as unsuitable for production. Which WSGI server is the standard replacement — and how does it consume a factory?
scenarios.prompt: How should this Flask app be served in production?
scenarios.situation: A Flask app currently runs via app.run in production.
scenarios.title: Flask behind a real server
scenarios.why: app.run is Werkzeug's development server — single-process, no hardening, not built for production traffic. Gunicorn is the standard WSGI server: gunicorn 'myapp:create_app()' (or a wsgi.py exposing app) with multiple workers, typically behind nginx. The factory pattern composes fine with gunicorn's import string.

choices: Hardcode the database URL in settings.py — it's the same for all environments
Read DATABASE_URL from the environment (os.environ) and fail fast with a clear error if it's missing — config varies per environment, code doesn't
Store the production database password in the repo's .env.example as documentation
Use SQLite in production too — one fewer moving part
scenarios.hint: Twelve-factor config: what varies between deploys goes in the environment. What's committed here that shouldn't be — and what breaks when staging needs a different database?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this database configuration?
scenarios.situation: Database credentials are hardcoded in settings.py and committed to git.
scenarios.title: Credentials in the repo
scenarios.why: Config that varies per environment (credentials, hosts, feature flags) belongs in environment variables, not source — committed secrets leak to every repo clone and can't differ between staging and production. The twelve-factor pattern: read DATABASE_URL / individual vars from the environment, fail fast at startup if required vars are missing, and keep .env.example as documentation with placeholder values only.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Python Web as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Framework Setup Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Framework Setup is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Framework Setup?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Framework Setup issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Framework Setup is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Framework Setup supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Framework Setup failure in Python Web.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Framework Setup
evidence: All Framework Setup components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

Escalate to senior support — Routing & Views is too complex to troubleshoot systematically

domains.name: Start Here
domains.description: How to use this bootcamp, study strategy for web developer interviews, and the web lab environment guide.

scenarios.title: Navigating the bootcamp
scenarios.situation: You're new to Python web dev and want to be interview-ready in 8 weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What's the right first two weeks?
choices: Read all 15 domains before coding
Start-here (all 4 lessons), then framework setup and routing/views in order — the request lifecycle first; everything else hangs off it
Jump to websockets — most exciting
Do mock interviews first
scenarios.why: The request lifecycle is the foundation: routing, views, and middleware are where every web question lives. Front-loading them builds the mental model everything assumes.
scenarios.hint: What mental model underlies every web question?

scenarios.title: Planning study time
scenarios.situation: You have 6 hours a week. You want to build real skill.
choices: 6h of lessons
All building, no theory
Cram at the end
2h lessons, 2h labs, 2h scenarios — web skill is building; labs create the muscle memory, scenarios train the architecture judgment interviews test
scenarios.why: Web development is a building discipline: the labs accumulate into real features, and scenarios train the system-design thinking. Theory without building doesn't transfer to interviews.
scenarios.hint: What do web interviews actually test?
evidence: Build every week; judgment via scenarios

scenarios.title: Using labs effectively
scenarios.situation: Labs build one evolving project. A lab's feature breaks the previous lab's tests.
choices: Fix forward: the broken tests caught a regression — debug it, fix the feature or update the tests deliberately; the suite is the safety net doing its job
Delete the failing tests
Skip the new feature
Start the project over
scenarios.why: Broken tests on a new feature are the suite working: either the feature regressed (fix it) or the contract changed (update tests deliberately). Deleting tests destroys the safety net the capstone needs.
scenarios.hint: What does a broken test tell you?
evidence: Red tests are information — fix forward

scenarios.title: Mock interview strategy
scenarios.situation: First mock: you can build features but fumble system-design questions.
choices: Memorize design answers
Avoid design questions
Drill system design separately: caching, scaling, async, data modeling — one design question per session, drawn as architecture diagrams; re-mock when you can whiteboard 3 designs fluently
More coding drills
scenarios.why: System design is a separate skill from coding: it needs diagram practice and trade-off articulation, not more route handlers. Targeted design drills close the specific gap the mock revealed.
scenarios.hint: What does the mock say to drill?

domains.name: Mock Assessment
domains.description: Timed assessment shell — scenarios are drawn from all domains at runtime.

domains.name: Capstone: Full-Stack App
domains.description: Design and build a complete full-stack web application: API, frontend integration, realtime features, tests, and deployment.

scenarios.title: Capstone: auth design
scenarios.situation: Phase 1: the API needs authentication for web and future mobile clients.
choices: No auth for the MVP
JWT bearer tokens — stateless, works for web + mobile, short expiry with refresh rotation; sessions are fine for web-only but don't extend to mobile cleanly
Session cookies only
API keys per user, never expiring
scenarios.why: JWT fits the multi-client future: stateless verification, mobile-friendly, with refresh rotation for security. Sessions tie you to cookie clients; perpetual API keys are a breach waiting to happen.
scenarios.hint: What client types must the auth serve?
evidence: JWT + refresh rotation for multi-client APIs

scenarios.title: Capstone: realtime scope
scenarios.situation: Phase 2: which features actually need realtime vs polling?
choices: Everything via polling
Realtime for digests too

Realtime (WebSocket): task assignments, comments, presence — user-facing live collaboration. Polling/background: digests, exports, notifications log — realtime where immediacy matters, async where it doesn't
Everything via WebSocket
scenarios.why: Realtime is a cost (connections, complexity) — spend it where immediacy is the feature (collaboration). Digests and exports are inherently async; websockets add nothing but load.
scenarios.hint: What makes a feature need realtime?
evidence: Realtime for collaboration; async for the rest

scenarios.title: Capstone: scaling plan
scenarios.situation: Launch: 100 users. If it grows 100x, what breaks first?
choices: Rewrite in another language
Add more servers blindly

Database queries (N+1 on task lists), then websocket connection count per server, then background job throughput — name the bottlenecks in order with the fix for each (eager loading, sticky/channel scaling, worker count)
Nothing — it will scale linearly
scenarios.why: Scaling analysis names bottlenecks in failure order with fixes: N+1 queries die first (fix: eager loading/pagination), then connection fan-out, then job throughput. 'More servers' without analysis scales the bottleneck too.
scenarios.hint: What usually breaks first in web apps?
evidence: Name bottlenecks in order, with fixes

scenarios.title: Capstone: testing the realtime layer
scenarios.situation: Phase 3: how do you test WebSocket notifications?
choices: Manual browser testing only
Skip — realtime is hard to test
Test the HTTP API only
Test client websocket connections: connect as two users, trigger an assignment, assert the other receives the message — plus auth rejection tests (no token = no connection) and reconnect behavior
scenarios.why: Realtime is testable: the test client speaks websocket, so the full flow (connect, subscribe, trigger, receive) runs in the suite. Auth and reconnect are the edge cases that break in production.
scenarios.hint: What are the realtime edge cases?
evidence: Full WS flow in-suite: connect, trigger, receive, auth, reconnect

scenarios.title: Capstone: the demo
scenarios.situation: Demo day: 5 minutes for the full-stack app.
choices: CI logs
Live flow: create a task, assign it — the assignee's screen updates live (realtime!), comment appears, email arrives — the app's magic in 2 minutes; then architecture (API, WS, workers) in 2; Q&A
Code walkthrough
Architecture diagrams only
scenarios.why: Demo the magic: the live realtime flow IS the product story — assignment appearing on another screen sells the whole build. Architecture follows as the 'how it's built right' proof.
scenarios.hint: What sells a full-stack app in 2 minutes?
evidence: Live realtime flow first, architecture second

domains.name: REST APIs
domains.description: REST design, versioning, pagination, error handling, and API documentation with Python frameworks.

scenarios.title: Breaking change
scenarios.situation: You must rename a widely-used field in the API response.
choices: Ship /v2/ with the new field, keep /v1/ stable, announce deprecation with a 6-month sunset, document the migration — breaking changes are product events, not commits
Rename in place — clients will adapt
Add the new field, remove old immediately
Never change anything
scenarios.why: API consumers are customers: versioning + sunset + migration docs respects them. In-place renames break clients silently; immediate removal breaks them loudly.
scenarios.hint: Who is affected by a breaking change?

scenarios.title: Deep pagination
scenarios.situation: An endpoint with offset pagination slows down at page 10,000.
choices: Cursor/keyset pagination (where id > last_seen) — stable performance at any depth, no skipped/duplicated rows on concurrent writes; keep offset for shallow internal use
Bigger database
Cache all pages
Limit to 100 pages
scenarios.why: Offset reads and discards N rows — cost grows with depth. Keyset seeks directly to the position: O(1) per page regardless of depth, and stable under concurrent writes.
scenarios.hint: Why does offset degrade with depth?
evidence: Cursor for depth; offset only when shallow

scenarios.title: Duplicate charges
scenarios.situation: Clients retry POST /payments on timeouts; double charges occur.
choices: Tell clients not to retry
Faster payments (fewer timeouts)
Dedupe by amount + user
Idempotency-Key header: store key -> response on first success, replay the stored response on retry — retries become safe; the key makes the operation idempotent
scenarios.why: Network retries are normal — the API must tolerate them. Idempotency keys make retried requests return the original result instead of repeating the side effect. Client discipline doesn't fix server semantics.
scenarios.hint: What makes a retried POST safe?
evidence: Key -> stored response; replays, never re-executes

scenarios.title: Inconsistent errors
scenarios.situation: Each endpoint returns errors in a different shape; mobile clients parse them with regexes.
choices: Adopt RFC 7807 problem details uniformly: {type, title, status, detail} + field errors — one shape, machine-readable codes, documented in OpenAPI; migrate endpoint by endpoint
Document the 12 existing shapes
Return 200 with error strings
GraphQL instead
scenarios.why: Error consistency is a contract: clients branch on codes, humans read messages. RFC 7807 is the standard shape — adopting it uniformly kills the regex parsing.
scenarios.hint: What do clients need from errors?

scenarios.title: Chatty API
scenarios.situation: The mobile app makes 50 requests to render one screen.
choices: Faster network
More caching
It's the client's problem

Design for the client: dedicated endpoints or field selection (?fields=) returning the screen's data in 1-2 requests — or evaluate whether the client's needs justify a BFF (backend-for-frontend) layer
scenarios.why: Chatty APIs push latency onto the client: 50 round trips dominate load time. Server-side aggregation (screen-shaped endpoints, field selection) collapses the trips. The API serves clients, not tables.
scenarios.hint: What dominates the screen's load time?

scenarios.title: API key leak
scenarios.situation: A customer's API key appears in a public repo.
choices: Revoke immediately, issue a replacement, audit usage for abuse, and review key hygiene (scoped, prefixed, rotatable) — leaked keys are compromised keys, no exceptions
Ask them to delete the repo
Monitor for abuse first
It's a free-tier key — ignore
scenarios.why: Leaked credentials are compromised the moment they're public — revocation is the first action, not monitoring. The incident also audits the key lifecycle that allowed a long-lived unscoped key.
scenarios.hint: What's the first action on a leaked key?
evidence: Revoke first, audit second, improve hygiene third

scenarios.title: Undocumented API
scenarios.situation: The API works but has no docs; integrators keep asking questions.
choices: Write a wiki page once
Answer questions as they come
Record a video walkthrough
Generate OpenAPI from the code (models + docstrings), add descriptions and examples, publish Swagger UI — docs derived from code stay in sync; handwritten docs rot
scenarios.why: Docs from code (OpenAPI generation) stay accurate because they can't drift — the models ARE the documentation source. Wikis rot; videos can't be searched; Q&A doesn't scale.
scenarios.hint: Why do generated docs beat wikis?
evidence: Generate from code — accuracy by construction

domains.name: Async Tasks
domains.description: Background jobs, Celery, task queues, scheduling, and async processing patterns.

scenarios.title: Sync or job?
scenarios.situation: New feature: on signup, send welcome email, generate avatar thumbnails, sync to CRM.
choices: Cron job scanning for new users
Request: validate + create user + return 201 immediately. Jobs: welcome email, thumbnails, CRM sync — each a separate idempotent task with retries; the request never waits for them
All in the request — simpler
Email in request, rest in jobs
scenarios.why: The request does the minimum (validate + persist + respond); everything slow or flaky becomes jobs. Separate tasks per concern — email failure shouldn't block thumbnails. 201 now, work async.
scenarios.hint: What stays in the request cycle?

scenarios.title: Flaky third party
scenarios.situation: The CRM API fails 10% of the time with 503s.
choices: Idempotent task with exponential backoff retries (max 5), then dead-letter — transient 503s succeed on retry; the DLQ catches the truly broken for human review
Retry forever
Fail immediately — data loss acceptable
Call synchronously instead
scenarios.why: Classify the failure: 503 is transient (retry with backoff), persistent failure goes to DLQ (not infinite retry, not silent drop). Idempotency makes retries safe.
scenarios.hint: How do you classify 503 vs 400 here?

scenarios.title: Missed schedules
scenarios.situation: The nightly report sometimes doesn't run; beat logs show gaps.
choices: More workers
It's fine — mostly runs
Beat liveness first (single scheduler? process alive? monitored?), then schedule definition (timezone? DST?), then worker capacity at 2 AM — silent scheduler death is the usual suspect
Run it manually each morning
scenarios.why: Periodic work needs scheduler monitoring: duplicate beats double-fire, dead beats silently stop everything. Liveness checks + single-scheduler guarantees come before any other theory.
scenarios.hint: What's the usual suspect for missed periodic tasks?

scenarios.title: Double processing
scenarios.situation: A payment webhook task sometimes runs twice, double-crediting accounts.
choices: Faster task (smaller window)
Hope webhooks arrive once
Lock the whole table
Idempotent handler: keyed by the webhook's event ID — check processed-events before acting (atomic check-and-set); at-least-once delivery is normal, double-processing is the bug
scenarios.why: At-least-once delivery means duplicates WILL happen — the handler must tolerate them. Event-ID-keyed idempotency (processed set, atomic) makes the second delivery a no-op.
scenarios.hint: What delivery guarantee do webhooks actually provide?

scenarios.title: Growing queue
scenarios.situation: Queue depth grows steadily; workers are at 100% CPU.
choices: Bigger workers
Ignore — queues drain eventually
Delete old tasks

Bash script with curl

scenarios.title: Socket auth

Accept all, check later
IP whitelist only
Obscure URL path

scenarios.situation: The notification service must hold 10k concurrent connections.
choices: Long-lived HTTP requests
Multiple app servers with Redis pub/sub fan-out (any server publishes, all servers push to their connections), stateless connection handling, load-tested per-server capacity — the horizontal pattern
One big server
Polling instead

scenarios.situation: Feature: live dashboard of system metrics (server -> browser only).
choices: Websockets — more modern
Polling every second
WebRTC

scenarios.title: Slow consumer
scenarios.situation: One dashboard client on a slow connection; the broadcast buffer grows.
choices: Slow the broadcast for everyone
Bigger server
Bounded per-connection buffer — drop or disconnect the laggard past the bound; one slow client must not stall the broadcaster or OOM the server
Unbounded buffer — it'll catch up
scenarios.why: Backpressure is per-connection: the laggard gets dropped/disconnected, the system stays healthy. Unbounded buffers trade one slow client for server memory; slowing everyone punishes the healthy.

scenarios.title: Dropped connections
scenarios.situation: Mobile clients drop connections frequently (tunnels, elevators).
choices: Reconnect without resume (miss messages)
Keep-alive pings only
Exponential backoff reconnect + last-event-id resume + server-side per-channel backlog — the client catches up on what it missed, automatically
Show an error, require manual refresh

Client-reported presence, trusted

Poll the database

Re-run until green
Delete it

Run tests sequentially
Fewer tests
Mock the database everywhere

scenarios.title: Permission matrix
scenarios.situation: An endpoint leaked another user's data in staging.

Code review only

Trust the framework

Bigger servers, hope
Launch and watch
Rate-limit everyone

Skip tests on feature branches
Accept it

Slack the frontend team on changes

Email them a temporary password

lessons.title: Framework Setup — Core concepts
concepts: Startapp only scaffolds files; Django's app registry learns about the app through INSTALLED_APPS in settings.py (add 'inventory' or 'inventory.apps.InventoryConfig').
INSTALLED_APPS: check the class actually exists in that module, then look at INSTALLED_APPS and import cycles. --fake-initial is for migration state, not missing classes.
App factory: with a factory, you point it at the callable using the module:factory syntax — FLASK_APP=shop:create_app (optionally with arguments, e.g. shop:create_app('development')).
flask run: the Flask CLI imports the value of FLASK_APP.

pip: a committed requirements file with pinned versions (pip freeze or, better, pip-tools compile producing a lock file) plus a documented venv setup makes installs deterministic. pip resolved to a different Python than the venv's — the venv was created but never activated, so pip installed into the system (or another) environment.

example.code:
def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.register_blueprint(bp)
    return app

# no module-level `app` object
example.walkthrough: The Flask CLI imports the value of FLASK_APP. The factory pattern stays valuable for testing and multiple instances; you just have to tell the CLI where the factory lives.

pitfalls: Common trap: flask 3 removed the app factory pattern; define the app at module level instead.
Common trap: run migrate --fake so Django believes the field exists without touching the database.
Common trap: flask must be installed with apt, not pip, on Debian-based systems.
Common trap: run collectstatic so the app's models are registered with the ORM.

lessons.title: Routing & Views — Core concepts
concepts: URL dispatch: (The url_prefix affects the URL path, not the endpoint name — a common confusion.). request.args holds the query string (?a=b in the URL); request.form holds parsed POST form bodies; request.get_json() handles JSON payloads.

Path() converters (<int:year>, <slug:slug>, <uuid:pk>, <str:name>, <path:rest>) both validate the segment and convert it to the Python type before the view runs; non-matching URLs fall through to a 404.
url_for: when a view is registered on a blueprint named 'admin', its endpoint becomes 'admin.dashboard' — the blueprint name prefixes the function name. url_for must use the full endpoint.
Request data: the principle: serialize to JSON-safe types before handing data to the response.

example.code:
def year_archive(request, year):
    # year arrives as a string; /archive/abcd/ should 404 but doesn't
example.walkthrough: path() converters (<int:year>, <slug:slug>, <uuid:pk>, <str:name>, <path:rest>) both validate the segment and convert it to the Python type before the view runs; non-matching URLs fall through to a 404. Without a converter, every segment is a string and validation becomes manual view code.

pitfalls: Common trap: redirects must be returned from middleware; views can only return 200 responses.
Common trap: jsonResponse only accepts lists; wrap the dict in a list.
Common trap: use redirect() but with status_code=200 so the browser stays on the same page.
Common trap: url_for can't reverse blueprint routes.

lessons.title: Models & ORM — Core concepts
concepts: ForeignKey: accessing book.author on each iteration lazily fires one query per book — the N+1 problem. select_related('author') follows the ForeignKey with a SQL JOIN, loading authors in the initial query.
N+1 queries: picking the right variant is part of writing correct queries, not just fast ones.

Field lookups: django field lookups come in case-sensitive/case-insensitive pairs: contains/icontains, exact/iexact, startswith/istartswith. contains maps to LIKE (case behavior depends on the database collation — Postgres LIKE is case-sensitive), while icontains forces case-insensitive matching.

example.code:
def register(request):
    # TODO: duplicate-email handling
example.walkthrough: An exists() check followed by an insert is a check-then-act race: two concurrent requests can both see 'no such email' and both insert. The database unique constraint is the real enforcement — it raises IntegrityError on the loser. The correct pattern: validate early in the form for a friendly message, and catch IntegrityError at save time for the race. unique=True creates the constraint; it doesn't replace handling the exception.

pitfalls: Common trap: add unique=True to the email field.
Common trap: querySets hit the database when defined, so the loop is fine.
Common trap: foreignKeys don't need on_delete in Django 5.
Common trap: each iteration issues a query (N+1).

lessons.title: Templates & Forms — Core concepts
concepts: XSS: jinja2 autoescapes {{ }} output in Flask templates, so HTML in the bio shows as harmless text — that's the protection working. |safe marks content as trusted HTML, and applying it to user input re-enables stored XSS.
CSRF: (Flask-WTF adds CSRF protection to the form automatically.).

Templates: {% extends %} / {% block %} is Django's layout mechanism: base.html defines the skeleton with named blocks, child templates override only what differs. {% include %} composes static partials but can't be overridden per page; context processors supply variables, not markup.
Autoescape: django autoescapes variable output by default: <script> becomes <script> and renders as inert text.

Forms: django forms encapsulate the whole input pipeline: field types convert strings to Python values (IntegerField rejects 'abc'), validators enforce rules, is_valid() gates processing, cleaned_data provides the converted values, and the form re-renders with per-field errors.
Validation: this avoids hand-assigning dozens of fields and keeps validation in one place.

The page is safe as written — the danger enters only if someone applies |safe or mark_safe to user content. The review checklist: user content must never pass through |safe; that's the single gate between data and code execution here.

lessons.title: Auth & Security — Core concepts
concepts: Password storage: plaintext storage, reversible encryption, and fast hashes like MD5 all fail the moment the database leaks: fast hashes fall to brute force in hours.
SQL injection: string-interpolating user input into SQL is textbook SQL injection: crafted input escapes the string literal and rewrites the query.
Parameterized queries (placeholders + params list) send the SQL and the values separately, so input can never become code.

def sign_in(request):
    # TODO: verify username/password and start a session

The pair is the standard flow — hand-rolled cookie user-ids skip session signing, rotation, and backend abstraction. @login_required on protected views completes the triangle.

lessons.title: Deploy & Scale — Core concepts
concepts: WSGI servers: production Django is gunicorn (or uvicorn for ASGI) running the WSGI callable with multiple workers, behind nginx handling TLS termination, static files, and request buffering. Gunicorn is the standard WSGI server: gunicorn 'myapp:create_app()' (or a wsgi.py exposing app) with multiple workers, typically behind nginx.
Runserver is a development convenience: single-threaded, no security hardening, inefficient static handling, and it literally warns against production use.

Production Django needs the trio: DEBUG=False (tracebacks leak settings, paths, and queries), ALLOWED_HOSTS set to the real hostnames (Django 400s everything else once DEBUG is off — Host header attack defense), and SECRET_KEY plus DB credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager, never committed.

Secrets: ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] and committed secrets each quietly undo one of these protections. Config that varies per environment (credentials, hosts, feature flags) belongs in environment variables, not source — committed secrets leak to every repo clone and can't differ between staging and production.

example.code:
from myapp import create_app
app = create_app()
example.walkthrough: app.run is Werkzeug's development server — single-process, no hardening, not built for production traffic. The factory pattern composes fine with gunicorn's import string.

pitfalls: Common trap: static files are served from each app's static/ directory automatically in production.
Common trap: serve static files from Django and skip the reverse proxy to reduce moving parts.
Common trap: run migrations by hand on the production database whenever someone remembers.
Common trap: migrations run automatically when gunicorn starts.

lessons.title: Python Web Development — Core concepts
concepts: Flask is a minimal WSGI framework: you add routing, templates, and extensions yourself, which keeps small apps simple but leaves structure to you. FastAPI is async-first and uses Python type hints plus Pydantic models to get request validation, serialization, and OpenAPI docs from the same declarations.

REST maps resources to URLs and HTTP verbs: GET reads, POST creates (201 Created + Location), PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes (204 No Content). Status codes are part of the contract — 4xx means the client must change something, 5xx means the server failed.

ORMs like SQLAlchemy map rows to objects so you write Python instead of SQL, but the abstraction leaks: lazy-loaded relationships cause N+1 queries, and the fix is eager loading (joinedload/selectinload or select_related) plus reading the actual SQL during development.

Authentication proves who the caller is; authorization decides what they may do. For browser and mobile clients, short-lived signed JWT access tokens with rotating server-side refresh tokens scale across instances while still allowing revocation.

Tests form a pyramid: many fast unit tests (pure logic, fakes for I/O), fewer integration tests against a real database with per-test rollback, and a thin layer of end-to-end tests. Order-dependent tests are a bug in the suite, not the code.

Never trust the framework to save you from the basics: validate and escape output to stop XSS, parameterize every query (the ORM does this by default — raw SQL must too), store passwords with a real KDF like bcrypt/argon2 via passlib, and keep secrets in environment variables, not source.

example.walkthrough: The Item model declares the expected JSON shape; FastAPI validates the request body against it and returns a 422 with details on bad input. The same model generates the OpenAPI schema, so interactive docs stay in sync with the code for free.

pitfalls: Common trap: returning 200 for everything — clients and caches rely on 201/204/404/409 semantics.
Common trap: N+1 queries from lazy ORM relationships — eager-load and check the query log before shipping list endpoints.
Common trap: putting secrets or JWT signing keys in source control — use environment variables and rotate compromised keys.
Common trap: blocking calls (sync ORM, requests) inside async endpoints — they stall the whole event loop.

See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Models & ORM to the broader Models & ORM ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Models & ORM begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Models & ORM. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Models & ORM as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full Models & ORM flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: This bootcamp has 15 domains: 6 core web domains, 5 advanced domains, plus start-here, capstone, mock assessment, and exam prep. Work them in order — framework setup before routing, routing before models.
Lessons teach concepts with working code; scenarios test architecture judgment; labs build real features. The mock assessment pulls scenarios from every domain under time pressure.
Web interviews test whether you can build and reason about complete systems — not just write routes. Every scenario is a system decision; the capstone proves you can ship.
Track readiness per domain: 80%+ on scenario sets before moving on. The exam-prep domain loops back to weak areas — plan for two passes, not one.

example.code: Week 1: start-here + framework + routing. Week 2: models + templates/forms + auth. Week 3: REST + async + websockets + testing + capstone. Week 4: exam-prep + mocks to 85%+.
example.walkthrough: Your 4-week arc: framework core, advanced web, then prove it.

pitfalls: Skipping framework fundamentals — everything assumes them.
Reading without building — labs are where it sticks.
lessons.try_it: Set up your web lab environment today

lessons.title: Study Strategy for Web Interviews
concepts: Web interviews test: framework fluency (request lifecycle, ORM, auth), API design (REST, status codes, versioning), system design (caching, scaling, async), and practical skills (testing, deployment, debugging).
Learn in dependency order: framework -> routing -> models -> forms/templates -> auth -> deployment -> advanced (REST depth, async, realtime, testing). Each layer assumes the previous.
For every feature, know: the request lifecycle it participates in, the idiomatic usage, one security consideration, and how it scales. 'How does auth work end-to-end' beats 'what is a decorator'.
Build a 'request lifecycle' mental model: request -> routing -> middleware -> view -> ORM -> response. Every web question maps to a stage — know each stage cold.

example.code: Lifecycle: WSGI/ASGI server -> middleware (auth, CORS) -> router -> view (validation, logic) -> ORM (queries) -> serializer -> response. Trace every feature through it.
example.walkthrough: Draw the request lifecycle for your framework from memory.

pitfalls: Studying features in isolation from the lifecycle.
Ignoring the security angle per feature.
lessons.try_it: Trace a login request through all lifecycle stages

lessons.title: Course Roadmap Overview
concepts: Core domains (1-6): framework setup, routing/views, models/ORM, templates/forms, auth/security, deploy/scale — the working web developer's toolkit. These six are the interview's center of gravity.
Advanced domains (7-11): REST APIs, async tasks, websockets/realtime, web testing, plus exam-prep — the professional layer, and the capstone that proves you can build full-stack.
Capstone: a full-stack app — REST API, realtime notifications, background jobs, tested, deployed. It's the portfolio piece — 'I shipped this' beats 'I studied this'.
Systems-anatomy runs alongside as your reference for how the web stack runs (servers, processes, protocols). Consult it when behavior confuses you.

example.code: Core (6) -> Advanced (4) -> Capstone -> Exam-prep -> Mocks. Systems-anatomy alongside as reference.
example.walkthrough: Map your experience to the roadmap — where's your weakest core domain?

pitfalls: Jumping to websockets before routing is solid.
