lessons.title: Terminal and Lab Guide for Web
concepts: Labs build a real web app incrementally. The pattern: implement a feature, test it with curl/the test client, break it, fix it. Every lab states its endpoint and verification.
Environment: Python 3.10+, venv, your framework (FastAPI/Django/Flask per lab), pytest, httpx for API tests. One venv for the whole web track — it's one evolving project.
Lab hygiene: git init from day one, commit per lab, .env for secrets (never committed). The labs accumulate into the capstone — treat them as real development.
Testing tools: curl for quick checks, the framework's test client for API tests, browser devtools for frontend integration. Verify at the HTTP layer — that's the contract.

example.code: python3 -m venv ~/workspace/cbt-build/web-venv && ~/workspace/cbt-build/web-venv/bin/pip install fastapi uvicorn pytest httpx && echo web-env-ready
example.walkthrough: Create the web venv with framework + test tools.

lessons.try_it: Create the web venv and run a hello-world API

lessons.title: Phase 1: API and Data Model
concepts: The capstone builds a team task board: projects, tasks, comments, assignments — with realtime updates and email notifications. Phase 1: data model + REST API with auth.
Data model: User, Project, Task (status workflow: todo -> doing -> done), Comment. Relationships via the ORM; migrations from day one — schema evolves, migrations track it.
API: RESTful routes with JWT auth, pagination on lists, filtering (status, assignee), proper status codes. The API contract documented (OpenAPI) — frontend and tests consume the docs.
Deliverable: working API with auth, tested endpoints (happy + error paths), OpenAPI docs. The foundation the realtime and async layers build on.

example.walkthrough: Filtered, paginated, authenticated list — the API pattern repeated everywhere.

pitfalls: No auth on the API 'for now'.
lessons.try_it: Design your data model and route table

lessons.title: Phase 2: Realtime and Background Jobs
concepts: Phase 2 adds life: WebSocket notifications (task assigned -> instant update), background jobs (email notifications via Celery, digest emails on schedule). The app becomes interactive.
Realtime design: WebSocket per user, channel per project — users subscribe to their projects' channels. Connection auth via JWT; heartbeat for liveness; reconnection handled client-side.

Background jobs: Celery + Redis — send_email tasks (retry on failure), nightly digest (scheduled beat), heavy exports (async, notify on completion). The request cycle stays fast; work moves to workers.
Failure design: job retries with backoff, dead-letter queue for poison tasks, idempotent handlers (duplicate delivery is normal). Async systems fail differently — design for it.

example.walkthrough: Retry with exponential backoff — the async failure pattern.

pitfalls: Long work in the request cycle.
lessons.try_it: Design your realtime channels + job topology

lessons.title: Phase 3: Testing, Hardening, Ship
concepts: Phase 3 makes it production: API tests (90%+), websocket tests, load test (k6/locust) establishing the baseline, security pass (authz on every route, input validation, rate limiting), then deploy.

Security checklist: authentication on all routes, authorization (users see only their projects), validation on all inputs, rate limits on auth endpoints, secrets in env, security headers. Check each, document each.
Load test: establish the baseline (requests/sec at p99 < 500ms), find the bottleneck (usually DB queries — N+1), fix, re-test. Numbers before launch, not after.
Deliverable: deployed app URL, test suite green in CI, load-test report, security checklist signed, README + demo. Ship it like a product — because it is one.

example.code: pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=90 && ruff check . && echo SHIP-READY
example.walkthrough: The ship gate: tests green, coverage met, lint clean.

lessons.try_it: Run the security checklist on your API

lessons.title: Choosing and Setting Up the Framework
concepts: Framework choice: FastAPI (modern API, async, auto-docs), Django (batteries-included, ORM+admin), Flask (minimal, flexible). Match to the project: API service -> FastAPI; content CMS -> Django; microservice -> Flask.
Project layout: src/ package, tests/, pyproject.toml, .env, README. The layout IS the onboarding — new developers navigate by convention, not archaeology.

Dev server vs production server: the dev server (uvicorn --reload, flask run) is for development; production needs a real server (uvicorn workers, gunicorn) behind a reverse proxy. Never serve prod from the dev server.
Settings: environment-based config (dev/staging/prod), secrets from env vars, DEBUG off in prod. The settings module is the deployment contract.

example.code: mkdir taskboard && cd taskboard && python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install fastapi uvicorn && echo setup-done
example.walkthrough: Scaffold the project: venv + framework — the starting line.

lessons.try_it: Scaffold a project with proper layout

lessons.title: WSGI vs ASGI and Server Choice
concepts: WSGI (sync) vs ASGI (async): WSGI handles one request per worker at a time; ASGI supports async views and websockets. Choose ASGI for realtime/async features, WSGI for classic sync apps.
Servers: uvicorn (ASGI), gunicorn (WSGI, sync workers) or gunicorn+uvicorn workers (best of both). Workers = parallelism: 2-4 x CPU cores, tuned by workload.
Reverse proxy (nginx): TLS termination, static files, rate limiting, buffering slow clients. The app server serves the app; nginx serves the internet — separate concerns.
The interview answer: 'uvicorn workers behind nginx, ASGI for our websocket features' — the stack named with reasons.

example.code: .venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --workers 4 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
example.walkthrough: Production-style server: 4 workers, all interfaces.

pitfalls: App server directly on the internet.
lessons.try_it: Choose the server stack for 3 app profiles

lessons.title: Middleware: Auth, CORS, Logging
concepts: Middleware wraps every request: authentication (who), CORS (who may call from browsers), logging (what happened), rate limiting (how much). Order matters — auth before views, CORS early.
CORS: browsers enforce it; the server declares allowed origins. Development allows localhost; production lists exact domains. CORS '*' with credentials is the security bug.
Request logging middleware: method, path, status, duration — the access log. Structured (JSON) for aggregation. Every request logged, sampled at high volume.
Custom middleware: timing headers, request IDs (trace through logs), maintenance mode. Small, focused, tested — middleware is global code, bugs are global too.

example.code:
@app.middleware('http')
async def add_request_id(request, call_next):
    rid = uuid4().hex
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers['X-Request-ID'] = rid
    return response
example.walkthrough: Request-ID middleware: trace every request through the logs.

lessons.title: Configuration and Environments
concepts: Environment parity: dev/staging/prod run the same code, different config. The config surface: database URLs, secret keys, feature flags, external service endpoints.
pydantic-settings: typed config from env vars — Settings(db_url: str, debug: bool = False). Validation at startup: misconfiguration fails fast, not at 3 AM.
Feature flags: decouple deploy from release — ship dark, enable per environment/user. The flag service (or env var for simple cases) is the rollout control.
Secrets: env vars or a secret manager, never code. Rotation: the app reads at startup (or watches); document the rotation procedure.

example.code:
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str
    secret_key: str
    debug: bool = False
    class Config: env_file = '.env'
example.walkthrough: Typed settings: validation at startup, .env for local dev.

pitfalls: if PROD: config scattered through code.
lessons.try_it: Set up typed settings for 3 environments

lessons.title: Routing: URLs to Views
concepts: Routes map URLs to view functions: @app.get('/tasks/{task_id}') — path parameters typed (int, str), query parameters for filters, the route table IS the API surface.
Route order matters: specific before general ('/tasks/new' before '/tasks/{id}'), or the parameter swallows the literal. The classic 404-that-shouldn't-be.
RESTful conventions: nouns not verbs (/tasks not /getTasks), plural collections, nested for relationships (/projects/{id}/tasks). Consistency is the API's UX.
Versioning: URL path (/v1/tasks) for breaking changes — the pragmatic default. Header versioning is purer; URL versioning is clearer. Pick one, document it.

example.walkthrough: Nested RESTful route with optional filter — the collection pattern.

lessons.try_it: Design the route table for the capstone

lessons.title: Views: Thin Handlers
concepts: Views are HTTP adapters: parse input, call the service layer, return the response. Business logic lives in services, not views — views are thin by discipline.
Dependency injection: Depends(get_db), Depends(get_current_user) — the framework wires resources; views declare needs. Testable: override dependencies in tests.
Response models: response_model=TaskOut — the view declares its contract; the framework validates and documents. Internal models never leak to clients.
Error translation: service exceptions -> HTTP status (NotFound -> 404, Validation -> 422). The view is the exception translator — one place, consistent mapping.

example.walkthrough: Thin view: validate (framework), delegate (service), translate (exceptions).

lessons.try_it: Refactor a fat view into view + service

lessons.title: Request Validation
concepts: Validation at the boundary: pydantic models for bodies, typed parameters for paths/queries. Invalid input rejected with 422 before touching business logic — the gate.
Model design: TaskIn (creation fields) vs TaskOut (response, includes id/timestamps) vs TaskUpdate (all optional). Separate models per direction — the API's type safety.
Custom validators: @field_validator for cross-field rules ('due date after start'), constr for patterns. Business rules in validators are testable without HTTP.
Error messages: clear, field-specific ('priority must be 1-5'). Clients fix what they understand — validation errors are user interface.

example.walkthrough: Validated input model: constraints + custom rules, tested without HTTP.

lessons.title: Response Shaping and Status Codes
concepts: Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created (with Location header), 204 No Content (deletes), 400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 422 validation, 500 server error. The vocabulary — use it precisely.
Response envelopes: consistent shape {'data': ..., 'meta': {...}} vs bare resources. Pick one; document it. Pagination meta (page, total, next) in the envelope.
Content negotiation: JSON by default; the Accept header for variants. Version in URL, format in headers — separate concerns.
Error responses: consistent {'error': {'code': 'NOT_FOUND', 'message': ...}} — machine-readable code + human message. Clients branch on codes, humans read messages.

example.walkthrough: 201 + Location + envelope — the creation response done right.

lessons.title: Middleware Ordering and Guards
concepts: Middleware order: exception handlers outermost, then CORS, then auth, then logging, then rate limiting. Wrong order = auth errors without CORS headers (browser confusion).
Route guards: dependencies as guards — Depends(require_admin) on admin routes. Declarative protection at the route level, not if-statements in views.
Rate limiting: per-endpoint limits (login: 5/min, API: 100/min) — slow brute force, preserve UX. 429 with Retry-After header — the standard.
Timeouts: view-level timeouts for slow operations; the server's global timeout as backstop. Hung views consume workers — bound them.

example.walkthrough: Guard as dependency: declarative, testable, reusable.

pitfalls: No rate limiting on auth endpoints.
lessons.try_it: Add guards + rate limits to 3 routes

lessons.title: Modeling with the ORM
concepts: Models are Python classes mapping to tables: class Task(Base): __tablename__, Columns with types, relationships. The model IS the schema definition — migrations derive from it.
Relationships: ForeignKey + relationship() — Task.project, Project.tasks. back_populates for bidirection; lazy loading strategies (selectin for lists — kills N+1).
Column types: String(200), Integer, DateTime(timezone=True), Enum, JSON. Match the type to the data — the DB enforces what the model declares.
Constraints in models: unique=True, nullable=False, CheckConstraint — the schema enforces integrity, not just the app. Defense in depth for data.

example.code:
class Task(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'tasks'
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    title = Column(String(200), nullable=False)
    project_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey('projects.id'))
    project = relationship('Project', back_populates='tasks')
example.walkthrough: Model with FK + relationship — the relational mapping in Python.

lessons.title: Queries: From Simple to Complex
concepts: Session queries: session.query(Task).filter(...).all() or select(Task).where(...) (2.0 style). Learn the 2.0 select() style — it's the future and the interview expects it.
Filtering: ==, .in_(), .like(), and_/or_ combinations. Eager loading: selectinload(Task.project) — the N+1 killer, applied deliberately per query.
Aggregations: func.count(), group_by — reports in the ORM. Pagination: .offset().limit() or keyset (where id > last) for large lists.
The N+1: accessing task.project in a loop fires a query per task — selectinload upfront. Every list endpoint gets the N+1 review.

example.code:
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload
stmt = (select(Task).options(selectinload(Task.project))
          .where(Task.status == 'todo').limit(50))
example.walkthrough: Eager loading in the query — N+1 prevented at the source.

lessons.title: Migrations
concepts: Migrations version the schema: alembic revision --autogenerate, review the script, alembic upgrade head. Autogenerate is a draft — REVIEW it (it misses renames, data migrations).
Migration discipline: one migration per change, reversible (downgrade tested), never edit applied migrations. Production migrations run in deploy — tested in staging first.
Data migrations: separate from schema (backfill in batches, not one giant UPDATE). Large tables migrate in chunks with progress logging — the zero-downtime pattern.
The interview question: 'how do you add a non-nullable column to a 100M-row table?' — add nullable, backfill in batches, then set not-null. Three steps, no downtime.

example.code:
# migration: add nullable, backfill, then constrain
# op.add_column('tasks', sa.Column('priority', sa.Integer(), nullable=True))
# ... backfill batches ...
# op.alter_column('tasks', 'priority', nullable=False)
example.walkthrough: The big-table pattern: nullable -> backfill -> constrain.

lessons.try_it: Write a reversible migration with data backfill

lessons.title: Transactions and Sessions
concepts: Session = unit of work: add objects, commit once. Request-scoped sessions (one per request, closed after) — the web pattern. Never share sessions across requests/threads.
Transaction boundaries: the request is the transaction (commit on success, rollback on exception). Long transactions hold locks — keep views fast, move slow work to background jobs.
Isolation: default read-committed suffices for most; explicit locking (with_for_update) for read-modify-write (counters, inventory). Lost updates need the lock.
Session lifecycle in the framework: dependency yields session, closes after response. The pattern prevents leaked connections — connection pools are finite.

example.walkthrough: Request-scoped session: open, yield, guaranteed close.

lessons.title: Performance: Indexing and Query Tuning
concepts: Index foreign keys and filter columns: project_id, status, (status, due_date) composites. The ORM doesn't auto-index FKs in all backends — declare indexes explicitly.
EXPLAIN the slow queries: the ORM generates SQL — log it, explain it, index it. ORM abstraction doesn't exempt query tuning.
Bulk operations: bulk_insert_mappings for loads (not one add() per row). Read-only queries: yield_per for streaming large results — constant memory.
Caching: query-result caching (Redis) for hot reads; the ORM's identity map is per-session, not a cache. Cache at the service layer with invalidation.

example.code:
class Task(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'tasks'
    # ...
    __table_args__ = (Index('ix_task_project_status', 'project_id', 'status'),)
example.walkthrough: Composite index declared on the model — the query planner's friend.

pitfalls: One add() per row for bulk loads.
lessons.try_it: Index 3 query patterns; verify with EXPLAIN

lessons.title: Templates: Rendering HTML
concepts: Templates separate presentation from logic: Jinja2 (Flask/FastAPI) or Django templates. Variables {{ }}, control {% %}, inheritance (base.html blocks) — DRY for pages.
Template inheritance: base layout (nav, footer) with {% block content %} — pages fill blocks. One base, many pages — consistent UI without duplication.
Autoescaping: templates escape variables by default — the XSS defense. |safe only for trusted HTML (and then, rarely). Autoescape off is the vulnerability.
Logic in templates: minimal — loops, conditionals, filters. Complex logic belongs in views/context processors. Templates are dumb by design.

example.walkthrough: Inheritance: base layout once, pages fill the blocks.

lessons.title: Forms: Handling User Input
concepts: Forms: render, validate, redisplay with errors. Server-side validation ALWAYS (client JS is UX, not security) — the framework's form library or pydantic models.
CSRF protection: tokens on state-changing forms — the framework generates, the template includes, the view verifies. Missing CSRF is the finding.
Error display: field-level errors next to fields, form-level for cross-field. Users fix what they see — validation UX is part of the feature.
File uploads: size limits, type validation (not just extension), storage outside web root, virus scanning for user content. Uploads are the attack surface — treat them so.

example.walkthrough: Declarative form validation — rules as code, errors automatic.

lessons.try_it: Build a validated form with CSRF

lessons.title: HTMX and Modern Patterns
concepts: HTMX: HTML-driven interactivity — hx-get/hx-post swap fragments, no SPA framework. Server renders HTML fragments; the page updates surgically. The simplicity answer for dynamic UIs.
When HTMX vs SPA: content-driven apps with sprinkles of interactivity -> HTMX; complex client state -> SPA + API. Match the architecture to the interaction complexity.
Fragment endpoints: views returning partial templates for HTMX requests (detect via HX-Request header). Same view, full page or fragment — content negotiation.
Progressive enhancement: works without JS (forms post normally), enhanced with HTMX. Resilience by default — the JS-optional baseline.

example.code:
<button hx-post='/tasks/1/complete' hx-swap='outerHTML'>
  Complete
</button>
example.walkthrough: One attribute set makes the button dynamic — no JS written.

lessons.title: Static Files and Assets
concepts: Static files: CSS/JS/images served efficiently — WhiteNoise for simple, CDN + hashed filenames for production. Hashed names (app.a1b2.css) enable far-future caching.
Collect/build: the framework collects static into one dir; the CDN serves it. Versioned filenames bust caches on deploy — no stale CSS mysteries.
Media uploads: user files go to object storage (S3/GCS), not the app server — served via CDN with signed URLs for private content. Local disk uploads don't scale or survive.
Compression: gzip/brotli at the proxy/CDN — text assets shrink 70%+. The performance freebie everyone forgets.

example.code: python -m whitenoise --help 2>/dev/null; echo 'static strategy: hashed names + CDN'
example.walkthrough: Static strategy: hash, cache far-future, serve via CDN.

lessons.title: SEO and Meta Basics
concepts: SEO fundamentals: semantic HTML, title/meta descriptions per page, canonical URLs, sitemap.xml, robots.txt. Server-rendered pages are SEO-native — the SSR advantage.
Meta tags: Open Graph + Twitter cards for link previews — title, description, image per page. Social sharing is free distribution; missing tags waste it.
Performance IS SEO: Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP) affect ranking. Fast server responses + optimized assets = ranking + UX.
Structured data: JSON-LD for rich results (articles, products, events). The 10-line addition that earns search features.

example.code:
<meta property='og:title' content='{{ task.title }}'>
<meta property='og:description' content='{{ task.summary }}'>
<script type='application/ld+json'>{"@type": "Task"}</script>
example.walkthrough: OG tags + JSON-LD per page — the SEO baseline.

lessons.try_it: Add SEO tags to 3 page types

lessons.title: Authentication: Sessions vs Tokens
concepts: Sessions: server-side state, cookie reference — revocable, but needs shared storage to scale. Tokens (JWT): stateless, scalable, but revocation needs a denylist.
Choose: web-only monolith -> sessions (simple, revocable); API + mobile/SPA -> JWT (stateless, multi-client). The client landscape decides.
JWT structure: header.payload.signature — claims (sub, exp, iat). Short access expiry (15min) + refresh rotation. Never store sensitive data in claims (they're readable).
Password storage: bcrypt/argon2 with per-user salts — never SHA, never plain. The framework's hasher (werkzeug, passlib) — don't roll your own.

example.code:
from passlib.context import CryptContext
pwd = CryptContext(schemes=['bcrypt'], deprecated='auto')
hashed = pwd.hash('secret')
assert pwd.verify('secret', hashed)
example.walkthrough: bcrypt via passlib: salted, adaptive — the password standard.

lessons.title: Authorization: Who Can Do What
concepts: Authentication (who) vs authorization (what): login proves identity; every endpoint must check permission. Auth without authz is the breach.
Patterns: role-based (admin/user), ownership (users see own projects), object-level (project members see the project). Check at the view AND the query (filter by permission).
The query-level check: list_tasks filters by user's projects — even if the view guard is bypassed, the data layer enforces. Defense in depth for data access.
IDOR: /tasks/42 accessed by non-member — the test. Every object endpoint gets the ownership check; every list gets the scope filter. Systematic, not hopeful.

example.walkthrough: Ownership in the query: non-members get 404 (not 403 — no info leak).

pitfalls: Checks only in views, not queries.

lessons.title: Common Web Vulnerabilities
concepts: OWASP for Python web: injection (parameterize — the ORM does it; raw SQL carefully), XSS (autoescape + |safe discipline), CSRF (tokens), broken auth (above), sensitive exposure (error messages, debug pages).
SQL injection via ORM: safe by default (parameterized); raw SQL with f-strings is the hole — use text() with bound params. Audit every raw query.
XSS: autoescaped templates + Content-Security-Policy header — defense in depth. User HTML needs sanitization (bleach) or markdown with a safe renderer.
Security headers: HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, CSP — set via middleware/proxy. The 5-minute hardening with outsized effect.

example.code:
# safe raw SQL: bound parameters, never f-strings
result = db.execute(text('SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE status = :s'), {'s': status})
example.walkthrough: Bound parameters in raw SQL — the injection-proof pattern.

lessons.try_it: Audit an app for the OWASP top 5

lessons.title: Rate Limiting and Abuse Prevention
concepts: Rate limiting: per-IP and per-user limits on auth endpoints (5/min login), API quotas (1000/hour), with 429 + Retry-After. Slow brute force to uselessness.
Implementation: Redis-backed counters (sliding window), middleware or decorator. In-memory limits don't survive multiple workers — shared state needed.
Beyond rate limits: account lockout (with care — user enumeration), CAPTCHA on abuse signals, alerting on spikes. Layered abuse prevention.
Enumeration: consistent responses for 'user not found' vs 'wrong password' — don't leak which half is right. Timing attacks: constant-time comparison for secrets.

example.walkthrough: Declarative rate limits — 5 logins/minute per IP.

lessons.try_it: Add rate limits to auth + API endpoints

lessons.title: Secrets and Config Security
concepts: Secrets: API keys, DB passwords, JWT signing keys — env vars or secret manager, never code/git. .env in .gitignore; .env.example documents the shape without values.
JWT keys: strong random (secrets.token_hex(32)), rotated periodically, different per environment. Key rotation procedure documented — the incident you plan for.
Dependency CVEs: pip-audit in CI — vulnerable web dependencies are the common breach vector. Update promptly; the web stack is a frequent target.
Error handling: generic 500s to clients, detailed logs server-side. Stack traces to users are information disclosure — the debug page left on in prod.

example.code: python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))"
example.walkthrough: Generate a real secret — 256 bits, no patterns.

lessons.title: Deployment Topologies
concepts: Topology: reverse proxy (nginx) -> app servers (uvicorn workers) -> DB + Redis. Each layer scales independently — the standard production shape.
Processes: systemd/supervisor for the app, or containers (Docker) orchestrated (compose for simple, k8s for scale). Containers package the environment — the reproducibility answer.
Zero-downtime deploys: rolling updates (new version up before old down), health checks gating the rollout, instant rollback (previous image). Deploy without fear.
The interview: draw the topology and explain each piece's job. 'Nginx terminates TLS and proxies to 4 uvicorn workers; Postgres + Redis behind' — the 30-second answer.

example.code: docker compose up -d --build  # app + db + redis, one command
example.walkthrough: Compose: the whole stack reproducible in one command.

lessons.title: Database in Production
concepts: Production DB: managed Postgres (RDS/Cloud SQL) over self-hosted — backups, patching, failover handled. The managed answer for most teams.
Connection pooling: PgBouncer or the driver's pool — web workers share limited DB connections. Pool size tuned: (workers x per-worker) <= max_connections.
Migrations in deploy: run before the new code starts (backward-compatible migrations), or expand/contract for zero-downtime. The deploy pipeline runs them — not a human at 2 AM.
Backups: automated daily + point-in-time recovery; TESTED restores. The backup exists when the restore works — calendar the drill.

example.code: echo 'pool: 20 connections, 4 workers x 5 each; migrations in CI deploy'
example.walkthrough: Pool math + migration discipline — the DB production rules.

lessons.title: Caching Strategies
concepts: Cache layers: browser (Cache-Control), CDN (static + cacheable pages), app cache (Redis for query results/sessions), DB query cache. Each layer has its invalidation story.
Redis patterns: cache-aside (app checks cache, falls back to DB, populates) — the standard. TTLs bound staleness; explicit invalidation on writes for correctness.
What to cache: hot read-heavy data (project lists, user profiles), expensive computations, sessions. Not: rapidly changing data, user-specific without keys.
Invalidation: the hard part — write-through or delete-on-write; versioned keys for deploys. 'There are only two hard things...' — have a strategy, not hope.

example.walkthrough: Cache-aside with TTL: check, fallback, populate — the pattern.

lessons.title: Observability for Web Apps
concepts: Logs: structured JSON to stdout, aggregated (the platform collects). Request IDs trace across services. ERROR with context — 'order failed' needs the order_id.
Metrics: request rate, error rate, p50/p99 latency, DB pool usage, queue depth — Prometheus format, dashboards, alarms on SLOs. The RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) per endpoint.
APM/tracing: distributed traces across API -> DB -> cache — the slow-request debugger. Sample in production (not every request).
Health endpoints: /health (liveness), /ready (dependencies up) — orchestrators and load balancers use them. The deploy safety mechanism.

example.walkthrough: Liveness vs readiness: alive vs able to serve — both needed.

lessons.title: Scaling Patterns
concepts: Horizontal scaling: stateless app servers behind a load balancer — sessions in Redis (not server memory), uploads in object storage. Statelessness is the scaling prerequisite.
Database scaling: read replicas for read-heavy, connection pooling, then sharding (the last resort — operational complexity explodes). Scale reads before restructuring writes.
Async offload: slow work to Celery workers — the request cycle stays fast. Worker count scales with queue depth (autoscale on queue length).
The interview: 'how would you handle 10x traffic?' — stateless + LB, cache hot paths, read replicas, async workers, then measure. Ordered by ROI, not hype.

example.code: 10x plan: 1) stateless + LB 2) Redis cache hot endpoints 3) read replica 4) Celery for slow work 5) load test to verify. Each step measured.
example.walkthrough: Ordered by ROI: the scaling playbook.

lessons.try_it: Write the 10x plan for the capstone

lessons.title: REST Design Principles
concepts: REST: resources (nouns), HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), stateless requests, uniform interface. The constraints that make APIs predictable and cacheable.
Resource modeling: /projects/{id}/tasks — nested for ownership, top-level /tasks with filters for cross-cutting queries. Both, deliberately: nesting for hierarchy, filters for search.
Statelessness: every request carries its auth; the server holds no session. Scalability's prerequisite — any server handles any request.
HATEOAS (brief): links in responses guiding clients — nice theory, rarely implemented fully. Know the term; pagination links are the pragmatic subset.

example.code:
# resource modeling
# GET /projects/5/tasks?status=todo&page=2
# nested ownership + filter + pagination in one URL
example.walkthrough: The URL tells the story: whose tasks, which subset, which page.

lessons.title: Versioning and Evolution
concepts: Versioning: /v1/ in the URL — the pragmatic standard. Breaking changes get a new version; old versions get a sunset timeline (6-12 months, communicated).
Backward-compatible evolution: additive changes (new fields, new optional params) don't need versions. Reserve versions for breaking changes (renames, removals, semantic shifts).
Sunset process: announce, document migration, warn via headers (Sunset, Deprecation), then remove. API consumers are customers — treat breaking changes as product events.
Contract testing: consumers' expectations encoded as tests against the API — breaking changes fail fast. The safety net for evolution.

example.walkthrough: Parallel versions: v1 stable while v2 evolves — the evolution pattern.

lessons.title: Pagination, Filtering, Sorting
concepts: Pagination: offset/limit (simple, deep-offset slow) vs cursor/keyset (where id > last, stable, fast). Public APIs offer cursor; internal can use offset. Document both.
Filtering: ?status=todo&assignee=5 — declarative query params, validated. Complex filters via a filter DSL or POST /search for query bodies.
Sorting: ?sort=-due_date,priority — minus for descending, comma for multi-key. Whitelist sortable fields — arbitrary sort keys are a DoS vector (unindexed sorts).
Response meta: {data: [...], meta: {page, per_page, total, next_cursor}} — clients paginate without guessing. The contract for list endpoints.

example.walkthrough: Cursor pagination + whitelisted sort — the production list endpoint.

lessons.title: Error Handling and Problem Details
concepts: RFC 7807 problem details: {type, title, status, detail, instance} — machine-readable errors. The standard your API should follow instead of inventing shapes.
Error taxonomy: client errors (4xx, fix the request), server errors (5xx, we broke). Validation details per field — {'title': ['required']} — so clients highlight fields.
Idempotency: POST retries create duplicates — Idempotency-Key header dedupes (store key -> response, replay on retry). Payment-ish endpoints need it.
Consistency: every error, same shape, same codes. The error contract is as important as the success contract — document both in OpenAPI.

example.walkthrough: Problem-details model: the standard error shape.

lessons.title: API Documentation with OpenAPI
concepts: OpenAPI: the machine-readable contract — FastAPI generates it from your models; for others, write it. /docs (Swagger UI) for humans, /openapi.json for tooling.
Documentation quality: descriptions on every endpoint, examples on requests/responses, error responses documented. Generated docs are only as good as your models and docstrings.
Client generation: OpenAPI -> typed clients (openapi-generator). The contract becomes code — frontend and mobile stay in sync automatically.
Versioning the docs: /v1/docs, /v2/docs alongside the versions. Docs are part of the versioned contract.

example.code: curl -s localhost:8000/openapi.json | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(len(d['paths']), 'paths documented'"
example.walkthrough: Count documented paths — the docs coverage check.

lessons.title: Rate Limiting and API Governance
concepts: Rate limits: per-key quotas (1000/hour free, more paid), burst allowances (token bucket), headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After). The API's traffic contract.
Tiers: free/paid/enterprise limits — the business model in headers. Quota overages: 429 with upgrade path, not silent drops.
API keys: hashed storage, prefixed (sk_live_...), scoped per key, revocable, rotatable. Keys are credentials — the full lifecycle.
Governance: deprecation policy, changelog, status page, support channel. Professional APIs are products — operated, not just shipped.

example.code:
from slowapi import Limiter
limiter = Limiter(key_func=lambda: request.state.api_key_tier)
# tier-based limits: free 100/hr, pro 10000/hr
example.walkthrough: Tiered rate limits by API key — the governance pattern.

pitfalls: No rate limits on public API.
lessons.try_it: Design tiers + limits for an API

lessons.title: Why Background Jobs
concepts: The request cycle must be fast: < 500ms p99. Anything slower (emails, reports, image processing, webhooks) moves to background jobs — the user gets a response, the work continues.
The pattern: request validates + enqueues + returns 202 Accepted (with a status URL); worker processes; client polls or gets notified. Async by design, not by accident.
What belongs in jobs: notifications, exports, aggregations, third-party calls (slow/flaky), scheduled work. What stays sync: validation, auth, fast DB reads/writes.
Failure semantics: jobs retry (transient) or dead-letter (permanent); the request never depends on job success. Decoupled fate — the reliability principle.

example.walkthrough: 202 + status URL: the async contract — accepted, trackable.

lessons.title: Celery: Tasks and Workers
concepts: Celery: the Python task queue — @task decorated functions, workers consume from the broker (Redis/RabbitMQ), results in the backend. The standard for Django/Flask/FastAPI background work.
Task design: small, idempotent, serializable args (IDs not objects). Tasks are messages — keep them lean; the worker fetches the data.
Worker topology: queues per priority (default, high, low), worker concurrency tuned (prefork for CPU, gevent for I/O), autoscaling on queue depth.
Calling: .delay() (fire), .apply_async(countdown=60) (scheduled), chains/groups/chords for workflows. The canvas primitives compose pipelines.

example.walkthrough: Tasks take IDs: serializable, fresh data at execution.

lessons.try_it: Set up Celery + Redis + one task

lessons.title: Scheduling with Beat
concepts: Celery Beat: the scheduler — periodic tasks (nightly digests, hourly syncs, weekly reports) defined as schedules, executed by beat, run by workers. Separate the scheduling from the doing.
Schedules: crontab('0 2 * * *') for cron-like, timedelta for intervals. Timezone-aware (UTC internally) — the DST bug lives here.
Reliability: beat needs a single scheduler (or django-celery-beat with DB locking) — duplicate beats double-fire. Monitor beat liveness — silent scheduler death stops all periodic work.
Idempotent periodic tasks: 'process yesterday's data' by date parameter — reruns are safe. Time-windowed, not 'process new' — the correctness pattern.

example.walkthrough: Beat schedule: named, cron-timed, UTC — the periodic pattern.

lessons.title: Retries, Dead Letters, Monitoring
concepts: Retry policy: transient failures (network, 5xx) retry with exponential backoff + jitter; permanent (4xx, bad data) go straight to dead-letter. Classifying the error decides the path.
Dead-letter queue: poison tasks isolated for inspection — the alert fires, a human investigates, the queue doesn't block. Every system needs one.
Monitoring: queue depth (growing = under-provisioned), task duration p99, retry rate, dead-letter count — alarms on each. Flower for inspection; metrics for alerting.
Idempotency: tasks may run twice (retry after partial success) — design handlers to tolerate it (upsert not insert, check-then-act atomically). At-least-once is the reality.

example.walkthrough: Bounded retries with backoff — transient failures handled.

lessons.try_it: Design retry + DLQ for 3 task types

lessons.title: Task Workflows: Chains and Chords
concepts: Canvas primitives: chain (A -> B -> C, sequential), group (A, B, C in parallel), chord (group + callback when all done). Workflows as data — composable, inspectable.
Example: chord(fetch_prices.s(p) for p in products, aggregate.s()) — parallel fetch, then aggregate. The fan-out/fan-in pattern in one expression.
Error handling in workflows: chain stops on failure (by default); chord callback needs all-or-error policy. Design the failure semantics per workflow — don't accept defaults blindly.
When not Celery canvas: complex DAGs -> Airflow/Prefect; simple sequences -> chain. Match the orchestrator to the workflow complexity.

example.code:
from celery import chain, group
workflow = chain(
    fetch_data.s(),
    group(process_chunk.s(i) for i in range(8)),
    aggregate.s(),
)
example.walkthrough: Chain of group: fetch, parallel process, aggregate — the pipeline as code.

lessons.title: Alternatives: RQ, Dramatiq, ARQ
concepts: RQ (Redis Queue): simpler than Celery — @job decorated functions, Redis only. The 'I need a queue, not a platform' answer for small-to-medium needs.
Dramatiq: actor-model tasks, good defaults (retries, rate limits), less magic than Celery. The middle ground — opinionated where Celery is flexible.
ARQ: asyncio-native tasks — async workers for I/O-bound jobs. Pairs with FastAPI/asyncio stacks; the async-consistent choice.
Choosing: Celery for complex workflows/ecosystem; RQ for simplicity; ARQ for async stacks. The team's operational capacity matters — Celery needs more tending.

example.code:
# RQ: the simple version
from rq import Queue
q = Queue(connection=redis_conn)
q.enqueue(send_email, user_id)  # that's the whole API
example.walkthrough: RQ's API in 3 lines — simplicity as a feature.

pitfalls: Sync tasks in an async stack (blocking).

lessons.title: WebSocket Fundamentals
concepts: WebSocket: persistent bidirectional connection — HTTP upgrade handshake, then frames both ways. The server can PUSH — the fundamental break from request/response.
Lifecycle: connect (auth!) -> subscribe -> message loop -> disconnect (cleanup). Each phase needs handling: auth on connect, channel routing, heartbeat, graceful close.
When websockets: live collaboration, notifications, chat, dashboards, gaming. When not: request/response suffices (CRUD), or SSE fits (server->client only).
Framing: JSON messages with {type, payload} — typed events, versioned. The message contract, documented like the REST API.

example.code:
@app.websocket('/ws')
async def ws(websocket: WebSocket, token: str = Query(...)):
    user = verify(token)  # auth BEFORE accept
    await websocket.accept()
    ...
example.walkthrough: Auth before accept: no anonymous sockets — the security baseline.

lessons.title: Channels and Pub/Sub
concepts: Channels: users subscribe to topics (project:5, user:42) — messages route by channel. The server maintains channel -> connections; Redis pub/sub shares across servers.
Multi-server: sticky sessions OR shared pub/sub (Redis) — the latter scales: any server publishes, Redis fans out, each server pushes to its connections. The scaling pattern.
Presence: who's online — heartbeat-tracked, channel-scoped. Join/leave events; stale presence cleaned by heartbeat timeout. The '3 collaborators viewing' feature.
Authorization per channel: subscription checks membership (project members only). Channel auth is the realtime IDOR — verify on subscribe, not just on HTTP.

example.code:
# Redis pub/sub fan-out across servers
await redis.publish(f'project:{pid}', json.dumps(event))
# each server: subscribed, pushes to its local connections
example.walkthrough: Redis as the cross-server bus — the scaling primitive.

lessons.title: Server-Sent Events (SSE)
concepts: SSE: server -> client text stream over HTTP — simpler than websockets (reconnect built-in, works through proxies). One-directional: the client can't send (use POST for that).
When SSE: notifications, live feeds, progress bars — server-push without client messages. Simpler ops than websockets; the pragmatic default for push-only.
Implementation: text/event-stream response, 'data: {...}\n\n' frames, client EventSource with auto-reconnect. The 20-line realtime feature.
Limits: 6 connections per browser per domain (HTTP/1.1), text-only. Many streams or binary -> websockets. Know the ceiling before choosing.

example.walkthrough: SSE endpoint: async generator as the event stream.

lessons.title: Realtime at Scale
concepts: Scaling websockets: connection count per server (10k-50k typical), sticky routing or shared pub/sub, horizontal server scaling behind the LB. Connections are the load — measure per-server capacity.
Backpressure: slow clients — buffer per connection (bounded!), drop or disconnect laggards. One slow client shouldn't stall the broadcaster.
State: connection state in Redis (not server memory) for failover — reconnects land anywhere. Ephemeral state is the scaling prerequisite.
Load testing realtime: k6/websocat swarms — establish max connections, message latency p99, behavior at saturation. Numbers before the launch, not after.

example.code: Capacity plan: 50k connections target / 10k per server = 5 servers + Redis bus + LB with IP hash (or shared pub/sub). Measured, not guessed.
example.walkthrough: Capacity math: connections per server -> server count.

lessons.title: Realtime Security
concepts: Auth: token on connect (query param or subprotocol), verified before accept. Re-auth on token expiry — short-lived tokens with refresh over the socket or reconnect.
Authorization: channel subscription checks membership every time — the realtime IDOR. Message handlers validate the sender may perform the action (not just the connection).
Abuse: rate-limit messages per connection (spam), max message size (memory), connection limits per user (exhaustion). Sockets are attack surface — treat them so.
Transport: wss:// (TLS) always in production — ws:// leaks tokens and messages. The handshake carries credentials; encrypt it.

example.code:
MAX_MSG = 64 * 1024
async for msg in websocket.iter_text():
    if len(msg) > MAX_MSG: await websocket.close(1009); break
    await handle(authenticated_user, msg)
example.walkthrough: Message size cap + auth context per handler — the socket firewall.

lessons.title: Fallbacks and Resilience
concepts: Fallbacks: websockets -> SSE -> long-polling — degrade gracefully where websockets are blocked (proxies, old clients). Feature-detect, don't assume.
Reconnection: client-side exponential backoff + jitter, resume with last-event-id (catch up on missed messages). The offline-tolerant client.
Missed messages: server-side per-channel backlog (Redis stream, last N) — reconnecting clients replay what they missed. At-least-once delivery for important events.
Testing resilience: kill connections mid-flow, block websockets (fallback engages?), server restarts (clients reconnect?). Chaos-test the realtime layer.

example.code:
# client: resume from last seen
last_id = localStorage.get('last_event_id')
source = new EventSource(`/events?since=${last_id}`)
example.walkthrough: Resume with last-event-id — the catch-up pattern.

lessons.title: The Testing Pyramid for Web Apps
concepts: Pyramid: unit (many, fast — model methods, validators, utilities) -> integration (medium — API endpoints against a test DB) -> e2e (few — critical user journeys in a browser). The ratio, not the religion.

What each level catches: units catch logic errors; integration catches contract mismatches (ORM queries, serializers); e2e catches 'it renders but the button does nothing'. Different bugs, different levels.
Anti-patterns: all-e2e (slow, flaky, expensive), no integration (units pass, the app 500s), testing the framework (don't test Django's router).
The pragmatic rule: if it's hard to unit-test, it needs integration coverage; if users can't complete the flow, e2e catches it. Coverage follows risk.

example.code:
# pyramid ratio example: 70/20/10
# tests/unit/test_pricing.py      <- fast, many
# tests/api/test_checkout.py     <- medium
# tests/e2e/test_purchase.py     <- few, critical path
example.walkthrough: Directory layout mirroring the pyramid: units many, e2e few.

lessons.try_it: Map your app to the pyramid

lessons.title: pytest Fixtures and Factories
concepts: Fixtures: @pytest.fixture for reusable setup (db session, test client, authenticated user) — scope function/class/session by cost. The test's supply chain.
Factories (factory_boy): UserFactory() with realistic defaults, traits for variants (admin=True). Faker data that reads like production — tests that catch real bugs.
Database fixtures: transactional tests (rollback per test, fast) vs truncate (slower, needed for some cases). Isolation per test — no test depends on another's data.
Parametrize: @pytest.mark.parametrize for input matrices — one test, many cases. The boundary-value battery, compact.

example.walkthrough: Auth client fixture: user + logged-in client in one fixture.

lessons.title: Testing API Endpoints
concepts: API tests: POST /tasks -> 201 + Location header; GET -> shape matches schema; invalid -> 422 with field errors. The contract, tested.
Auth coverage: unauthenticated -> 401, wrong user -> 403/404, happy path -> 200. Every endpoint, all three. The permission matrix, automated.
Test DB: separate database, migrations applied, transactions rolled back per test. Fast, isolated, realistic — the three properties of a good test DB.
Contract tests against OpenAPI: response shapes validated against the schema — the docs and the tests agree, enforced.

example.code:
def test_create_task(auth_client):
    r = auth_client.post('/tasks', json={'title': 'x'})
    assert r.status_code == 201
    assert r.json()['title'] == 'x'
example.walkthrough: API test: status + body — the contract assertion.

lessons.try_it: Write the permission matrix for 3 endpoints

lessons.title: Frontend and E2E Testing
concepts: E2E scope: critical journeys only (signup -> create -> pay) — the paths that must never break. Everything else belongs lower in the pyramid.
Playwright: modern e2e — auto-waiting, parallel, trace viewer for failures. The current standard; Selenium's successor for new projects.
Flakiness: the e2e tax — fix with deterministic waits (not sleeps), test data isolation, retry-once policies. Flaky tests get fixed or deleted — never tolerated.
Component tests: test interactive components (forms, tables) in isolation — the middle ground between unit and e2e for frontend-heavy features.

example.code:
# Playwright: critical journey
def test_purchase(page):
    page.goto('/pricing')
    page.click('text=Buy')
    expect(page).to_have_url('/checkout/success')
example.walkthrough: E2E as code: the purchase journey, asserted.

lessons.title: Load Testing Web Apps
concepts: Load testing: k6/Locust scripts hitting real endpoints — find the breaking point BEFORE users do. The capacity question, answered empirically.
What to measure: throughput (req/s), latency p95/p99, error rate, resource saturation (which tier breaks first). The four numbers of a load test.
Realistic scenarios: mix of endpoints weighted by production traffic, with think time. Hammering one endpoint measures nothing real.
Baseline + regression: run on schedule (nightly/weekly), alert on degradation. Performance is a feature — tested like one.

example.code:
# k6: realistic scenario
# http.get('/api/tasks'); sleep(1); http.post('/api/tasks', ...)
# stages: ramp 0->100 VUs over 5m, hold 10m
example.walkthrough: k6 stages: ramp, hold, measure — the load profile.

lessons.try_it: Script a load test for the capstone

lessons.title: CI/CD for Web Projects
concepts: Pipeline: lint -> unit -> integration -> build image -> security scan -> deploy staging -> e2e -> deploy prod. The gates in order; failures stop the line.
Speed: parallelize test shards, cache dependencies, run e2e only on main. The pipeline must be fast enough that developers don't bypass it.
Environments: dev (auto), staging (prod-like, seeded), prod. Migrations run as pipeline steps — forward-only, tested on staging first.
Quality gates: coverage floor on new code, zero critical vulns, e2e green. The gates encode the team's standards — automatic, not argued per-PR.

example.code: pytest -n auto --cov=app --cov-fail-under=80 -q  # parallel, coverage gate
example.walkthrough: Parallel tests with a coverage gate — the pipeline's unit stage.

pitfalls: Deploying on green unit tests alone.

lessons.title: Web Interview: Architecture Questions
concepts: 'Design a URL shortener' / 'Design Twitter': the interview classics — clarify requirements, estimate scale, draw components, drill into one hard part. The structured response.
What interviewers score: trade-off reasoning (why Postgres not Redis here), bottleneck identification, honest 'I'd need to look up' moments. Process over the perfect diagram.
Common drills: request lifecycle through your stack, auth flow end to end, 'what happens when this fails' for each component. The depth probes.
Preparation: build the capstone with these questions in mind — every decision documented becomes an interview answer. The project is the prep.

example.code: URL shortener drill: 100M URLs/month -> hash -> KV store (Dynamo-style) -> cache hot -> redirect 301. One paragraph, the architecture answer.
example.walkthrough: The drill answer format: scale, components, one hard part.

lessons.title: Web Interview: Code and Debug
concepts: Live coding: build a small endpoint or fix a broken one — interviewers watch the process (tests? edge cases? security?) not just the result.
Debug drills: 'this endpoint is slow' (profile: N+1? missing index? blocking call?), 'this is flaky' (race? shared state?), 'users report 500s' (read the traceback, reproduce, fix).
Talk through it: narrate the hypothesis, the check, the result. Silent coding hides your reasoning — the reasoning is what's scored.
Preparation: time-boxed practice on your own codebase — 45 minutes to add a feature with tests. The muscle memory of shipping under pressure.

example.code:
# debug drill: slow endpoint
# 1. EXPLAIN the query  2. check N+1 in logs
# 3. profile: cProfile or django-debug-toolbar
# hypothesis -> measure -> fix -> measure
example.walkthrough: The debug loop: hypothesis, measure, fix, measure.

lessons.title: System Design for Web Scale
concepts: The web-scale toolkit: LB -> stateless app tier -> cache -> DB (read replicas) -> queue -> workers. Drawn from memory, adapted to the problem.
Scaling levers: horizontal app tier, cache hit ratio, DB read/write split, async for slow work, CDN for static. Each lever has a 'when' — know the triggers.
Data at scale: sharding keys, hot partitions, eventual consistency trade-offs. The hard part of scale is state — interviewers drill here.
Numbers: 1M DAU, 100 req/s average, 10x peak — back-of-envelope math that grounds the design. Estimates before architecture.

example.code: 1M DAU, 5% concurrent = 50k sessions; avg 0.2 req/s/user = 10k req/s; 10x peak = 100k. Cache 80% -> 20k DB req/s -> read replicas. The estimation chain.
example.walkthrough: Back-of-envelope: users -> requests -> cache -> DB.

lessons.title: Security Interview Topics
concepts: The web security canon for interviews: OWASP Top 10 (current edition), auth flows (OAuth/OIDC), session vs token, CSRF/CORS, injection family, IDOR/BOLA. Know all, deep on three.
Scenario questions: 'design login securely' (hash, rate-limit, 2FA, session handling), 'review this code' (spot the vuln), 'we were breached' (response steps).
Defense framing: every attack question wants the mitigation — parameterized queries, output encoding, least privilege, the control for the threat.
Stay current: read one security writeup weekly — the field moves; interviews reward the recent example over the textbook answer.

example.code: 'Design secure login': bcrypt/argon2, rate-limit + lockout, 2FA option, HttpOnly Secure cookies, session rotation, audit log. Six controls, one answer.
example.walkthrough: The secure-login answer: six controls from memory.

lessons.title: Portfolio and Take-Home Projects
concepts: Take-homes: real-world simulations — build the thing well (tests, README, deployed link) but time-box it (the stated hours, not 40). Quality within bounds is the test.
What reviewers score: does it run (README that works), tests exist, code reads well, deployed demo. The first impression is 'it works on my click'.
Portfolio presentation: problem, decisions, trade-offs, what you'd do next. The README as the interview — reviewers read it before the code.
Boundaries: don't build the company's actual product for free; time-box visibly; ask clarifying questions first. Professional take-homes are scoped and respectful.

example.code: README template: problem -> run it (3 commands) -> decisions (3 bullets) -> trade-offs -> next steps. The take-home's first impression.
example.walkthrough: README structure that reviewers actually read.

lessons.title: The Final Review Sprint
concepts: Two weeks out: one mock interview (system design), one timed debug, one security scenario daily. The rotation that covers all formats.
One week out: capstone demo rehearsal (5 minutes, live), README review, the 'tell me about your project' answer memorized-but-natural.
The night before: logistics (link, ID, environment), sleep, no cramming. Performance is physiological — rest beats one more tutorial.
Interview day: arrive early, questions prepared for them (team, on-call, deploy process), follow-up note within 24h. The professional close.

example.code: Sprint plan: W1 mocks+drills daily; W2 demo rehearsal + project story; D-1 logistics+rest; D-day early + questions + follow-up. The final two weeks, scheduled.
example.walkthrough: The sprint as a schedule — concrete, dated.

simulations.brief: GET /dashboard/ returns 404, but the view exists and the dev server runs cleanly.

steps.symptom: GET /dashboard/ → 404. The view function dashboard exists.
evidence:
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('dashboard', views.dashboard),
]
options: Read the URL pattern: 'dashboard' has no trailing slash but the request asks for /dashboard/ — APPEND_SLASH behavior depends on the pattern

Add a second pattern without the slash

steps.symptom: Fix applied. Verify the route table.

simulations.title: Session or token?
simulations.brief: Choose the authentication mechanism for two different clients.

steps.text: Client 1 is a browser-based admin dashboard on the same domain. Mechanism?

choices.label: Cookie session: the browser sends it automatically, CSRF protection applies, logout is server-side
choices.feedback: Right: same-domain browser apps are the home turf of cookie sessions.

choices.label: Bearer token in localStorage
choices.feedback: Tokens in localStorage are XSS-readable; cookie sessions with httpOnly are safer here.

choices.label: HTTP Basic on every request
choices.feedback: Basic auth on every request exposes credentials constantly and can't expire cleanly.

steps.text: Client 2 is a mobile app calling the same API from another domain. Mechanism?

choices.label: Token (e.g. JWT): no cookies across domains, explicit expiry and revocation
choices.feedback: Right: cross-domain mobile clients can't rely on cookies — tokens travel in the Authorization header.

choices.label: Cookie session with CORS wide open
choices.feedback: Cross-domain cookies need SameSite=None; Secure plus precise CORS — fragile compared to tokens.

choices.label: No auth — it's just a mobile app
choices.feedback: Client type never determines auth need; the data's sensitivity does.

simulations.debrief: Same-domain browser → cookie sessions; cross-domain/mobile → tokens. Match the mechanism to the client's constraints, not to fashion.

sections.heading: Framework Setup
items: Startapp — Startapp only scaffolds files; Django's app registry learns about the app through INSTALLED_APPS in settings.py (add 'inventory' or 'inventory.apps.InventoryConfig').
INSTALLED_APPS — check the class actually exists in that module, then look at INSTALLED_APPS and import cycles. --fake-initial is for migration state, not missing classes.
App factory — with a factory, you point it at the callable using the module:factory syntax — FLASK_APP=shop:create_app (optionally with arguments, e.g. shop:create_app('development')).
Common trap — flask 3 removed the app factory pattern; define the app at module level instead.
Common trap — run migrate --fake so Django believes the field exists without touching the database.
Common trap — flask must be installed with apt, not pip, on Debian-based systems.
Common trap — run collectstatic so the app's models are registered with the ORM.
The Flask CLI — The Flask CLI imports the value of FLASK_APP. The factory pattern stays valuable for testing and multiple instances; you just have to tell the CLI where the factory lives.

sections.heading: Routing & Views
items: URL dispatch — (The url_prefix affects the URL path, not the endpoint name — a common confusion.). request.args holds the query string (?a=b in the URL); request.form holds parsed POST form bodies; request.get_json() handles JSON payloads.

Path() converters (<int — year>, <slug:slug>, <uuid:pk>, <str:name>, <path:rest>) both validate the segment and convert it to the Python type before the view runs; non-matching URLs fall through to a 404.
Request data — the principle: serialize to JSON-safe types before handing data to the response.
Common trap — redirects must be returned from middleware; views can only return 200 responses.
Common trap — jsonResponse only accepts lists; wrap the dict in a list.
Common trap — use redirect() but with status_code=200 so the browser stays on the same page.
